translated_text:
As for the “first category,” it occurs frequently in the writings of the Qarmatians and the philosophers who oppose the Muslims concerning the foundations of their religion. Whoever knows that Allah is pleased with the earliest forerunners and that they are pleased with Him knows that everything these people say to the contrary is false. Whoever acknowledges that the five daily prayers are obligatory upon everyone so long as they retain their reason knows that anyone who interprets a text as exempting some people from this obligation has fabricated a falsehood. Likewise, whoever knows that wine and indecent acts are forbidden to everyone so long as they retain their reason knows that anyone who interprets a text in a way that makes these things lawful for some people is fabricating a falsehood.

As for the “second category,” it often causes confusion for some people. The meaning may be correct, since the Quran and Sunnah substantiate it; the question, however, is whether the wording they cite actually conveys it. This falls into two subdivisions:

The “first” is to claim that this meaning is intended by the wording. This is fabricating a falsehood against Allah. Thus, whoever says that what is meant by His words, “slaughter a cow,” is the soul; by “Go to Pharaoh,” the heart; by “and those with him,” Abū Bakr; by “stern against the disbelievers,” ‘Umar; by “merciful among themselves,” ‘Uthmān; and by “You see them bowing and prostrating,” ‘Alī—has spoken falsely about Allah, whether deliberately or mistakenly.

The “second subdivision” is to treat this as a matter of drawing lessons and reasoning by analogy

rather than as a meaning conveyed by the wording. This is a form of analogy: what the jurists call analogy, the Sufis call allusion. This can be sound or unsound, just as analogy can.

Thus, suppose someone hears Allah’s words:

“None touch it except the purified,”

understands this to refer to the Preserved Tablet or a written copy of the Quran, and says: “Just as the Preserved Tablet, on which the letters of the Quran are written, is touched only by a pure body, so the meanings of the Quran are tasted only by pure hearts—the hearts of the God-fearing.” This is a sound meaning and a sound lesson to draw. Accordingly, this is reported from a number of the early generations. Allah Most High says:

“Alif Lām Mīm.”

“This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for the God-fearing.”

He also says:

“This is a clear statement to mankind, and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing.”

And:

“By it Allah guides those who seek His good pleasure to the ways of peace.”

There are other similar passages.

Likewise, someone may cite the saying:

“Angels do not enter a house containing a dog or a person in a state of major ritual impurity,”

and draw from it the lesson that the realities of faith do not enter a heart containing things that defile it, such as arrogance and envy. In this, he is correct. Allah Most High says:

“Those are the ones whose hearts Allah does not wish to purify.”

Allah Most High also says:

“I will turn away from My signs those who act arrogantly upon the earth without right. Even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. If they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as their way; but if they see the way of error, they will take it as their way.”

There are other similar passages.

The book Haqā’iq al-Tafsīr (The Realities of Quranic Exegesis), by Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī, contains three kinds of material:

First: reports whose attribution to those quoted is weak, such as most of what he transmits from Ja‘far al-Sādiq, much of which is falsely attributed to him. Most of the reports in the book stop at Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān himself. Experts have criticized Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān’s own transmission, to the point that, when al-Bayhaqī narrated from him, he would say: “He narrated to us from the original record of what he had heard.”

Second: reports that are authentically transmitted, but whose narrator was mistaken in what he said.

Third: authentic reports from someone whose statement is correct.

Every meaning that contradicts the Quran and Sunnah is false, and the argument supporting it is untenable. As for a meaning that accords with the Quran and Sunnah but is not what the wording intends, interpreting the wording by it is an error. If, however, it is mentioned by way of allusion, drawing a lesson, or analogy, it may be sound or unsound.

It is thus clear that whoever explains or interprets the Quran or hadith contrary to the interpretation known from the Companions and their Successors is fabricating lies against Allah, deviating concerning Allah’s signs, and distorting words from their proper places. This opens the door to heresy and impiety. That it is false is a matter of basic, indisputable knowledge in Islam.

Likewise, a group of Sufis claim that al-Hasan al-Basrī was his companion, and that ‘Alī entered the mosque and saw al-Hasan preaching among the storytellers. He asked him, “What makes religion sound?” He replied, “Scrupulousness.”

He asked, “And what corrupts it?” He replied, “Greed.” So he allowed him to remain and expelled the others.

Yet experts in transmitted reports agree that al-Hasan was not a companion of ‘Alī and learned nothing directly from him. Rather, he learned from his companions, such as al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, Qays ibn Sa‘d ibn ‘Abbād, and others like them. Al-Hasan did not preach during ‘Alī’s time, nor even during Mu‘āwiyah’s time; he only began doing so later.

People were already attributing lies to ‘Alī during his lifetime, to the point that people would question him about this. As established in the two Sahīhs, he was asked:

He replied, “No, by Him who split the seed and created the living soul, except this sheet.” It contains the ages of camels, the release of captives, and the stipulation that a Muslim is not to be killed for a disbeliever.

“And We will turn their hearts and eyes away, just as they did not believe in it the first time, and leave them wandering blindly in their transgression.”

That is: what will make you realize that when it comes, they will not believe in it, and We will turn their hearts away? In other words, they abandon faith, and We turn their hearts away because they did not believe the first time. That is, how do you know that both these things will not happen then?

Whoever understands the meaning of the verse will recognize the error of those who say that anna (“that”) means la‘alla (“perhaps”) and find the reading with an initial a-vowel problematic. Indeed, he will then recognize that it is better than the reading with an initial i-vowel. This is a broad subject.

People fall into three groups regarding this matter: two extremes and a middle course. One group claims that asceticism, purification of the heart, and discipline of the soul alone necessarily produce knowledge, without any other means.

Another group says that these have no effect; rather, knowledge is produced by knowing the scriptural or rational evidence.

The middle course is that these practices are among the greatest aids to attaining knowledge. Indeed, they are a prerequisite for acquiring much knowledge, but they are not sufficient on their own. Something else is indispensable: either knowledge of the evidence in matters that can only be known through it,

or a correct conception of the two terms of a proposition in matters of non-inferential knowledge.

As for the beneficial knowledge through which people are saved from the Fire and attain happiness, it can only be acquired by following the scriptures brought by the messengers. Allah Most High says:

“When guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor fall into misery.”

“But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We shall raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection.”

“He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’”

“He will say, ‘Thus it is: Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; likewise, today you will be forgotten.’”

“And thus We recompense whoever transgresses and does not believe,” and so on.

Allah Most High also says:

“Whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil who becomes his companion.”

Whoever thinks that guidance and faith can be attained merely by pursuing knowledge without acting upon it, or merely through practice and asceticism without knowledge, has gone astray. More astray than either is someone who, in pursuing knowledge and understanding, follows the path of the philosophers and speculative theologians without testing it against the Quran and Sunnah or acting as knowledge requires; or someone who, in practice and asceticism, follows the path of the philosophers and Sufis without testing it against the Quran and Sunnah or assessing practice in light of knowledge.

The latter have turned away from knowledge and revealed law, while the former have turned away from practice and revealed law. Each group has thus gone astray in these two respects. They have diverged greatly, until one group came to resemble the Jews who incurred divine wrath, and the other the Christians who went astray. Indeed, among both groups are some who have become worse

Section

As for the statement that “the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, assigned to each group what suited them,” and so forth, it admits of two interpretations.

If it means that prescribed deeds vary from person to person according to their circumstances, then there is no doubt about this. What the poor are commanded to do is not the same as what the wealthy are commanded to do; nor are the commands for the sick the same as those for the healthy. What is commanded in times of adversity differs from what is commanded when blessings are bestowed. A menstruating woman is not commanded to do the same as a woman who is ritually pure, nor are rulers commanded to do the same as their subjects. Thus, Allah’s commands to His servants may vary according to their circumstances, even as they may share the same foundation of faith in Allah, affirmation of His oneness, and belief in His Books and messengers.

If, however, it means that the Sharia itself varies, and that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, addressed Zayd with words contradicting what he said to ‘Amr, or disclosed to one person something contradicting what he disclosed to another—as the liars relate: “‘Ā’ishah asked him

 وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّ الْقَرَامِطَةَ وَأَمْثَالَهُمْ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ يَقُولُونَ:
 إنَّهُ أَظْهَرَ خِلَافَ مَا أَبْطَنَ وَأَنَّهُ خَاطَبَ الْعَامَّةَ بِأُمُورِ أَرَادَ بِهَا خِلَافَ مَا أَفْهَمَهُمْ لِأَجْلِ مَصْلَحَتِهِمْ؛ إذْ كَانَ لَا يُمْكِنُهُ صَلَاحُهُمْ إلَّا بِهَذَا الطَّرِيقِ وَقَدْ زَعَمَ ذَلِكَ ابْنُ سِينَا وَأَصْحَابُ 
" رَسَائِلِ إخْوَانِ الصَّفَا "
 وَأَمْثَالُهُمْ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَالْقَرَامِطَةِ الْبَاطِنِيَّةِ؛ فَإِنَّ ابْنَ سِينَا كَانَ هُوَ وَأَهْلُ بَيْتِهِ مِنْ أَتْبَاعِ الْحَاكِمِ القرمطي العبيدي الَّذِي كَانَ بِمِصْرِ. وَقَوْلُ هَؤُلَاءِ كَمَا أَنَّهُ مِنْ أَكْفَرِ الْأَقْوَالِ فَجَهْلُهُمْ مِنْ أَعْظَمِ الْجَهْلِ
translated_text:
‘Have you seen your Lord?’ He replied, ‘No.’ Abū Bakr asked him, and he replied, ‘Yes.’” And the claim that “he gave two contradictory answers to a single question because the two questioners’ circumstances differed”—all this is the speech of liars and fabricators; indeed, it is the speech of heretical hypocrites. For the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“It is not fitting for a prophet to give a treacherous glance.”

This hadith appears in Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere:

“In the year of the Conquest, he had declared the lives of several men forfeit, including Ibn Abī Sarh. ‘Uthmān brought him to pledge allegiance to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. He turned away from him twice or three times, then accepted his pledge. He then said, ‘Was there no man of sound judgment among you who, seeing me turn away from this man, would kill him?’ One of them said, ‘Why did you not signal to me with your eyes, O Messenger of Allah?’ He replied, ‘It is not fitting for a prophet to give a treacherous glance.’”

This emphatically affirms the complete agreement between his outward and inward states, his private and public conduct: he does not conceal anything contrary to what he outwardly displays, as scheming hypocrites habitually do.

There is no doubt that the Qarmatians and philosophers like them say that he outwardly displayed the opposite of what he concealed, and that he addressed the common people with statements by which he intended something contrary to what he led them to understand, for their own good, since he could reform them only by this means. Ibn Sīnā, the authors of the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity, and others like them among the philosophers and esoteric Qarmatians made this claim. Indeed, Ibn Sīnā and his household were followers of al-Hākim, the Qarmatian ‘Ubaydid ruler in Egypt. Just as their position is among the most flagrant expressions of disbelief, so too is their ignorance among the greatest.

original_text: وَذَلِكَ أَنَّهُ إذَا كَانَ الْأَمْرُ كَذَلِكَ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَعْلَمَهُ أَهْلُ الْعَقْلِ وَالذَّكَاءِ مِنْ النَّاسِ وَإِذَا عَلِمُوهُ امْتَنَعَ فِي الْعَادَةِ تَوَاطُؤُهُمْ عَلَى كِتْمَانِهِ كَمَا يَمْتَنِعُ تَوَاطُؤُهُمْ عَلَى الْكَذِبِ فَإِنَّهُ كَمَا يَمْتَنِعُ فِي الْعَادَةِ تَوَاطُؤُ الْجَمِيعِ عَلَى الْكَذِبِ يَمْتَنِعُ تَوَاطُؤُهُمْ عَلَى كِتْمَانِ مَا تَتَوَفَّرُ الْهِمَمُ وَالدَّوَاعِي عَلَى بَيَانِهِ وَذِكْرِهِ لَا سِيَّمَا مِثْلُ مَعْرِفَةِ هَذِهِ الْأُمُورِ الْعَظِيمَةِ الَّتِي مَعْرِفَتُهَا وَالتَّكَلُّمُ بِهَا مِنْ أَعْظَمِ مَا تَتَوَفَّرُ الْهِمَمُ وَالدَّوَاعِي عَلَيْهِ أَلَا تَرَى أَنَّ الْبَاطِنِيَّةَ وَنَحْوَهُمْ أَبْطَنُوا خِلَافَ مَا أَظْهَرُوهُ لِلنَّاسِ وَسَعَوْا فِي ذَلِكَ بِكُلِّ طَرِيقٍ وَتَوَاطَئُوا عَلَيْهِ مَا شَاءَ اللَّهُ. حَتَّى الْتَبَسَ أَمْرُهُمْ عَلَى كَثِيرٍ مِنْ أَتْبَاعِهِمْ. ثُمَّ إنَّهُمْ مَعَ ذَلِكَ اطَّلَعَ عَلَى حَقِيقَةِ أَمْرِهِمْ جَمِيعُ أَذْكِيَاءِ النَّاسِ مِنْ مُوَافَقِيهِمْ وَمُخَالِفِيهِمْ وَصَنَّفُوا الْكُتُبَ فِي كَشْفِ أَسْرَارِهِمْ وَرَفْعِ أَسْتَارِهِمْ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُمْ فِي الْبَاطِنِ حُرْمَةٌ عِنْدَ مَنْ عَرَفَ بَاطِنَهُمْ وَلَا ثِقَةٌ بِمَا يُخْبِرُونَ بِهِ وَلَا الْتِزَامُ طَاعَةٍ لِمَا يَأْمُرُونَ وَكَذَلِكَ مَنْ فِيهِ نَوْعٌ مِنْ هَذَا الْجِنْسِ. فَمَنْ سَلَكَ هَذِهِ السَّبِيلَ لَمْ يَبْقَ لِمَنْ عَلِمَ أَمْرَهُ ثِقَةٌ بِمَا يُخْبِرُ بِهِ وَبِمَا يَأْمُرُ بِهِ وَحِينَئِذٍ فَيُنْتَقَضُ عَلَيْهِ جَمِيعُ مَا خَاطَبَ بِهِ النَّاسَ فَإِنَّهُ مَا مِنْ خِطَابٍ يُخَاطِبُهُمْ بِهِ إلَّا وَيُجَوِّزُونَ عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَكُونَ أَرَادَ بِهِ غَيْرَ مَا أَظْهَرَهُ لَهُمْ فَلَا يَثِقُونَ بِأَخْبَارِهِ وَأَوَامِرِهِ فَيَخْتَلُّ عَلَيْهِ الْأَمْرُ كُلُّهُ فَيَكُونُ مَقْصُودُهُ صَلَاحَهُمْ فَيَعُودُ ذَلِكَ بِالْفَسَادِ الْعَظِيمِ؛ بَلْ كُلُّ مَنْ وَافَقَهُ فَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُظْهِرَ خِلَافَ مَا أَبْطَنَ كَاتِّبَاعِ مَنْ سَلَكَ هَذِهِ السَّبِيلَ مِنْ الْقَرَامِطَةِ
translated_text:
For if that were so, people of reason and intelligence would inevitably discover it. Once they knew it, their colluding to conceal it would be impossible in the ordinary course of events, just as their colluding to lie would be impossible. Just as universal collusion in lying is ordinarily impossible, so too is collusion in concealing something that people have strong motives and compelling reasons to explain and disclose. This applies especially to knowledge of such momentous matters, which people have the strongest motives and reasons to discover and discuss.

Do you not see that the esotericists and others like them concealed the opposite of what they outwardly presented to people, pursued every means of doing so, and colluded in it to whatever extent Allah willed, until their true nature became obscure even to many of their followers? Yet despite this, all intelligent people, supporters and opponents alike, discovered their true nature and wrote books exposing their secrets and lifting their veils. Those who knew their hidden reality had no inward respect for them, no trust in what they reported, and no commitment to obeying their commands. The same applies to anyone who displays anything of this kind.

Whoever follows this path loses the trust of those who know his true nature, both in what he reports and in what he commands. Everything he has said to people is then undermined, for whenever he addresses them, they consider it possible that he intends something other than what he outwardly conveys. They therefore trust neither his reports nor his commands, and his entire undertaking falls into disorder. His intention may be to reform them, but the result is grave corruption instead. Indeed, everyone who agrees with him must likewise outwardly display the opposite of what he conceals, as do the followers of those who have taken this path among the Qarmatians

original_text: الْبَاطِنِيَّةِ وَغَيْرِهِمْ لَا تَجِدُ أَحَدًا مِنْ مُوَافِقِيهِمْ إلَّا وَلَا بُدَّ أَنْ يُبَيِّنَ أَنَّ ظَاهِرَهُ خِلَافُ بَاطِنِهِ وَيَحْصُلُ لَهُمْ بِذَلِكَ مِنْ كَشْفِ الْأَسْرَارِ وَهَتْكِ الْأَسْتَارِ مَا يَصِيرُونَ بِهِ مِنْ شِرَارِ الْكُفَّارِ. وَإِذَا كَانَتْ الرُّسُلُ تُبْطِنُ خِلَافَ مَا تُظْهِرُ فَإِمَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ الْعِلْمُ بِهَذَا الِاخْتِلَافِ مُمْكِنًا لِغَيْرِهِمْ وَإِمَّا أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مُمْكِنًا كَانَ مُدَّعِي ذَلِكَ كَذَّابًا مُفْتَرِيًا؛ فَبَطَلَ قَوْلُ هَؤُلَاءِ الْمَلَاحِدَةِ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَالْقَرَامِطَةِ وَأَمْثَالِهِمْ وَإِنْ كَانَ الْعِلْمُ بِذَلِكَ مُمْكِنًا عَلِمَ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ مُخَالَفَةَ الْبَاطِنِ لِلظَّاهِرِ وَلَيْسَ لِمَنْ يَعْلَمُ ذَلِكَ حَدٌّ مَحْدُودٌ؛ بَلْ إذَا عَلِمَهُ هَذَا عَلَّمَهُ هَذَا وَعَلَّمَهُ هَذَا فَيَشِيعُ هَذَا وَيَظْهَرُ؛ وَلِهَذَا كَانَ مَنْ اعْتَقَدَ هَذَا فِي الْأَنْبِيَاءِ كَهَؤُلَاءِ الْبَاطِنِيَّةِ مِنْ الْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَالْقَرَامِطَةِ وَنَحْوِهِمْ مُعْرِضِينَ عَنْ حَقِيقَةِ خَبَرِهِ وَأَمْرِهِ لَا يَعْتَقِدُونَ بَاطِنَ مَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ وَلَا مَا أَمَرَ؛ بَلْ يَظْهَرُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ مُخَالَفَةِ أَمْرِهِ وَالْإِعْرَاضِ عَنْ خَبَرِهِ مَا يَظْهَرُ لِكُلِّ أَحَدٍ وَلَا تَجِدُ فِي أَهْلِ الْإِيمَانِ مَنْ يُحْسِنُ بِهِمْ الظَّنَّ؛ بَلْ يَظْهَرُ فِسْقُهُمْ وَنِفَاقُهُمْ لِعَوَامِّ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ فَضْلًا عَنْ خَوَاصِّهِمْ. وَأَيْضًا فَمَنْ كَانَتْ هَذِهِ حَالَهُ كَانَ خَوَاصُّهُ أَعْلَمَ النَّاسِ بِبَاطِنِهِ وَالْعِلْمُ بِذَلِكَ يُوجِبُ الِانْحِلَالَ فِي الْبَاطِنِ وَمَنْ عَلِمَ حَالَ خَاصَّةِ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ - كَأَبِي بَكْرٍ وَعُمَرَ وَغَيْرِهِمَا مِنْ السَّابِقِينَ الْأَوَّلِينَ - عَلِمَ أَنَّهُمْ كَانُوا أَعْظَمَ النَّاسِ تَصْدِيقًا لِبَاطِنِ أَمْرِ خَبَرِهِ وَظَاهِرِهِ وَطَاعَتَهُمْ
translated_text:
—the esotericists—and others. You will find that every one of their adherents inevitably reveals that his outward stance contradicts what he inwardly conceals. Their secrets are thereby exposed and their veils torn away, making them among the worst disbelievers.

If the messengers concealed the opposite of what they outwardly conveyed, then either others could discover this discrepancy or they could not. If discovering it were impossible, anyone claiming it would be a liar and a fabricator. Thus, the claim of these heretical philosophers, Qarmatians, and their like is invalid. If discovering it were possible, some people would learn that the inward reality contradicted the outward appearance. There would be no fixed limit to the number who could know this: once one person knew it, he would teach another, who would teach yet another, until it became widespread and openly known.

For this reason, those who hold such a belief about the prophets—such as these esotericists among the philosophers, Qarmatians, and their like—turn away from the true substance of his reports and commands. They believe neither in the inward truth of what he reported nor in what he commanded. Rather, their disobedience to his commands and disregard for his reports become apparent to everyone. You will find no believer who thinks well of them. Indeed, their wickedness and hypocrisy become apparent even to ordinary believers, let alone those of greater understanding.

Moreover, when someone is like this, his closest followers know his inward reality better than anyone else, and knowing it necessarily leads to an inward loss of commitment. Whoever knows the condition of the Prophet’s closest followers—Allah bless him and grant him peace—such as Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and the other earliest believers, knows that they were foremost among people in affirming the inward and outward truth of his message and in their obedience

original_text:
لَهُ فِي سِرِّهِمْ وَعَلَانِيَتِهِمْ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ أَحَدٌ مِنْهُمْ يَعْتَقِدُ فِي خَبَرِهِ وَأَمْرِهِ مَا يُنَاقِضُ ظَاهِرَ مَا بَيَّنَهُ لَهُمْ وَدَلَّهُمْ عَلَيْهِ وَأَرْشَدَهُمْ إلَيْهِ وَلِهَذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي الصَّحَابَةِ مَنْ تَأَوَّلَ شَيْئًا مِنْ نُصُوصِهِ عَلَى خِلَافِ مَا دَلَّ عَلَيْهِ لَا فِيمَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ اللَّهُ عَنْ أَسْمَائِهِ وَصِفَاتِهِ وَلَا فِيمَا أَخْبَرَ بِهِ عَمَّا بَعْدَ الْمَوْتِ وَأَنَّ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْ هَذَا مَا ظَهَرَ إلَّا مِمَّنْ هُوَ عِنْدَ الْأَئِمَّةِ مِنْ أَهْلِ النِّفَاقِ وَالِاتِّحَادِ كَالْقَرَامِطَةِ وَالْفَلَاسِفَةِ وَالْجَهْمِيَّة نفاة حَقَائِقِ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَالصِّفَاتِ. وَمِنْ تَمَامِ هَذَا أَنْ تَعْلَمَ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ لَمْ يَخُصَّ أَحَدًا مِنْ أَصْحَابِهِ بِخِطَابِ فِي عِلْمِ الدِّينِ قَصَدَ كِتْمَانَهُ عَنْ غَيْرِهِ وَلَكِنْ كَانَ قَدْ يَسْأَلُ الرَّجُلَ عَنْ الْمَسْأَلَةِ الَّتِي لَا يُمْكِنُ جَوَابُهَا؛ فَيُجِيبُهُ بِمَا يَنْفَعُهُ 
{كَالْأَعْرَابِيِّ الَّذِي سَأَلَهُ عَنْ السَّاعَةِ وَالسَّاعَةُ لَا يُعْلَمُ مَتَى هِيَ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 مَا أَعْدَدْت لَهَا؟ فَقَالَ مَا أَعْدَدْت لَهَا مِنْ كَثِيرِ عَمَلٍ؛
 وَلَكِنِّي أُحِبُّ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَقَالَ:
 الْمَرْءُ مَعَ مَنْ أَحَبَّ}
 فَأَجَابَهُ بِالْمَقْصُودِ مِنْ عِلْمِهِ بِالسَّاعَةِ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ يُخَاطِبُ أَصْحَابَهُ بِخِطَابِ لَا يَفْهَمُونَهُ؛
 بَلْ كَانَ بَعْضُهُمْ أَكْمَلَ فَهْمًا لِكَلَامِهِ مِنْ بَعْضٍ كَمَا فِي الصَّحِيحَيْنِ عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ قَالَ:
 {إنَّ عَبْدًا خَيَّرَهُ اللَّهُ بَيْنَ الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ فَاخْتَارَ ذَلِكَ الْعَبْدُ مَا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ؛
 فَبَكَى أَبُو بَكْرٍ وَقَالَ:
 بَلْ نَفْدِيك بِأَنْفُسِنَا وَأَمْوَالِنَا يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ فَجَعَلَ النَّاسُ يَعْجَبُونَ
translated_text:
to him, in private and in public. None of them held any belief about his reports or commands that contradicted the apparent meaning of what he had explained to them, indicated to them, and guided them towards. Thus, none of the Companions interpreted any of his statements contrary to what they indicated, whether concerning what Allah revealed about His names and attributes or what He revealed about events after death. Such interpretations arose only among those whom the leading scholars regarded as people of hypocrisy and the doctrine of union, such as the Qarmatians, the philosophers, and the Jahmiyyah, who deny the realities of the divine names and attributes.

To complete this discussion, you should know that the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—never singled out any of his Companions for instruction in religious knowledge that he intended to conceal from others. A man might, however, ask a question that could not be answered, and he would respond with something beneficial to him. For example:

This is among the most obvious fabrications. No Muslim scholar has transmitted it in any scholarly work. Its falsehood is plain, for ‘Umar is the best of this community after Abū Bakr. He was one inwardly addressed and inspired, upon whose tongue and heart Allah placed the truth. He is the foremost of those in this community who are addressed and inspired. If he was present, hearing the words, yet understood the conversation no better than a man of the Zanj, could anyone else conceivably have understood it better than he did? What, then, of someone who never heard the Messenger’s words, but merely asserts that the meanings he claims are those intended? Such an assertion would not be accepted even without evidence against it; how, then, when evidence establishes the falsehood of the person making it?

He related that a group of hypocrites had intended to loosen the girth of the Messenger of Allah’s camel at night so that he would fall from his mount and die. This was revealed to him, and Hudhayfah was nearby, so he secretly told him their names. It is said that ‘Umar would not offer the funeral prayer over anyone unless Hudhayfah did so.

None of this involves any of the truths of religion, nor any hidden meaning that contradicts the apparent meaning. Allah has described the hypocrites and related their deeds in His Book, so much so that Sūrat Barā’ah (Disavowal) was called “the Exposer” because it exposed the hypocrites. It was also called al-Muba‘thirah and given other names. Yet the Quran did not name particular individuals. If someone knows that certain individuals are among the hypocrites thus described, this is comparable to his knowing that certain individuals are among the believers promised Paradise. The Prophet’s declaration—Allah bless him and grant him peace—that Abū Bakr, ‘Umar, and others will be in Paradise is thus comparable to his declaration that those people were hypocrites. If this is considered hidden knowledge, it is hidden knowledge that agrees with the apparent meaning, confirms it, and corresponds to it.

Its counterpart in the sphere of commands is what is called “verifying the applicability of the ruling”: the Lawgiver makes a ruling contingent upon a particular attribute, and we ascertain that this attribute is present in a particular individual. Yet none of this involves any hidden meaning that contradicts the apparent meaning, nor even any of the truths of religion. Rather, that bag contained reports of the battles and tribulations that would occur. The battles are wars between Muslims and disbelievers, while the tribulations are conflicts among Muslims.

 وَلَمْ يَنْقُلْ أَحَدٌ قَطُّ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ حَدِيثًا يُوَافِقُ الْبَاطِنِيَّةَ وَلَا حَدِيثًا يُخَالِفُ الظَّاهِرَ الْمَعْلُومَ مِنْ الدِّينِ. وَمِنْ الْمَعْلُومِ أَنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ عِنْدَهُ شَيْءٌ مِنْ هَذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ بُدٌّ أَنْ يَنْقُلَ عَنْهُ أَحَدٌ شَيْئًا مِنْهُ بَلْ النُّقُولُ الْمُتَوَاتِرَةُ عَنْهُ كُلُّهَا تُصَدِّقُ مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْ الدِّينِ وَقَدْ رَوَى مِنْ أَحَادِيثِ صِفَاتِ اللَّهِ وَصِفَاتِ الْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ وَتَحْقِيقِ الْعِبَادَاتِ مَا يُوَافِقُ أُصُولَ أَهْلِ الْإِيمَانِ وَيُخَالِفُ قَوْلَ أَهْلِ الْبُهْتَانِ.
translated_text:
For this reason, ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Umar said:

“If Abū Hurayrah had told you that you would kill your caliph and do such and such, you would have said, ‘Abū Hurayrah has lied.’”

Disclosing such things is something kings and their supporters dislike, since it foretells changes in their rule. This is further clarified by the fact that Abū Hurayrah only embraced Islam in the year of Khaybar. He was therefore neither among the earliest Muslims nor among those who took the Pledge of Divine Pleasure. Other Companions knew more about the realities of religion than he did. The Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—would relate a hadith to him and others, and they would all hear it. Yet Abū Hurayrah retained hadith better than any of them, owing to a blessing he received through the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—for:

“One day, the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—was speaking to them and said, ‘Which of you will spread out his garment, so that he will forget nothing he has heard?’ Abū Hurayrah did so.”

It has also been reported:

“He used to divide the night into three parts: a third for prayer, a third for sleep, and a third for studying hadith.”

No one has ever transmitted from Abū Hurayrah any hadith that accords with the Bātiniyyah (esotericists), or any hadith that contradicts the known, apparent teachings of religion. It is evident that, had he possessed anything of this kind, someone would inevitably have transmitted some of it from him. Rather, the reports transmitted from him through so many channels as to establish certainty all affirm the apparent teachings of religion. He narrated hadiths concerning Allah’s attributes, the descriptions of the Last Day, and the proper fulfilment of acts of worship that accord with the principles of the people of faith and contradict the claims of the people of falsehood.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا مَا يُرْوَى عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الْخَرَّازِ وَأَمْثَالِهِ فِي هَذَا الْبَابِ وَمَا يَذْكُرُهُ أَبُو طَالِبٍ فِي كِتَابِهِ وَغَيْرُهُ وَكَلَامُ بَعْضِ الْمَشَايِخِ الَّذِي يَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ يَقُولُ بِبَاطِنِ يُخَالِفُ الظَّاهِرَ وَمَا يُوجَدُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ فِي كَلَامِ أَبِي حَامِدٍ الْغَزَالِيِّ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ.

" النُّور مِنْ كَلَامِ طيفور "
 فِيهِ شَيْءٌ كَثِيرٌ لَا رَيْبَ أَنَّهُ كَذِبٌ عَلَى أَبِي يَزِيدَ البسطامي وَفِيهِ أَشْيَاءُ مِنْ غَلَطِ أَبِي يَزِيدَ - رَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ - وَفِيهِ أَشْيَاءُ حَسَنَةٌ مِنْ كَلَامِ أَبِي يَزِيدَ وَكُلُّ أَحَدٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ يُؤْخَذُ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ وَيُتْرَكُ إلَّا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ.
وَمَنْ قِيلَ لَهُ عَنْ أَبِي يَزِيدَ أَوْ غَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْمَشَايِخِ:
 أَنَّهُ قَالَ لِمُرِيدِيهِ:
translated_text:
As for what is related from Abū Sa‘īd al-Kharrāz and others like him on this subject, what Abū Tālib mentions in his book and what others relate, the statements of certain shaykhs thought to affirm an inward meaning that contradicts the apparent meaning, and similar passages found in the writings of Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī or others—the answer to all this is as follows:

What is known to have come from the Messenger is conveyed by a trustworthy transmitter from an infallible speaker. Whatever contradicts it must be either a report from an unreliable transmitter or the statement of someone who is not infallible. Much of what is attributed to these men is falsely ascribed to them. In what is authentically reported from them, they were sometimes right and sometimes wrong. Most of their established statements employ broad, ambiguous expressions. Even had these been the words of the infallible Messenger, they would not have contradicted the established ruling. How much less, then, when they are the words of someone who is not infallible!

Abū al-Fadl al-Falakī compiled a book of the sayings of Abū Yazīd al-Bistāmī, which he entitled “Light from the Sayings of Tayfūr.” It contains much that was undoubtedly falsely attributed to Abū Yazīd al-Bistāmī. It also contains some errors made by Abū Yazīd—may Allah have mercy on him—and some good statements of his. Everyone’s statements may be accepted or rejected, except those of the Messenger of Allah—Allah bless him and grant him peace.

Anyone who is told that Abū Yazīd, or another of the shaykhs, said to his disciples:

translated_text:
“If you allow anyone from Muhammad’s community to enter the Fire, I disown you”—whereupon another challenged him, saying, “I told my disciples, ‘If you allow anyone from Muhammad’s community to enter the Fire, I disown you’”—and who believes this report about Abū Yazīd or another shaykh, then admires it and regards his spiritual standing as exalted, has shown his profound ignorance or hypocrisy.

For if he knows what the Messenger foretold—that some who commit major sins will enter the Fire, and that the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—will be the first whose intercession on their behalf is accepted, after intercession has been sought from the great messengers, such as Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, who will decline and offer their excuses—yet believes that the disciples of Abū Yazīd or another shaykh can prevent anyone from the community from entering the Fire, or that they themselves can bring out everyone who enters it, then he has disbelieved what the truthful and trustworthy Messenger foretold on the strength of a story whose transmitter lied, or whose original speaker was mistaken, if he was not deliberately lying. If, however, he does not know what the Messenger foretold, then he is among the most ignorant of people concerning the foundations of faith.

A Muslim must therefore hold firmly to the Quran and Sunnah and strive to attain certain knowledge of what the Messenger reported and commanded. He must then not abandon what is clear and known for what is ambiguous and unknown. That would be like someone travelling to Mecca along a known road which will undoubtedly take him there if he follows it, only to turn away from it onto an unknown road which he neither knows nor knows where it ends. Such is the case of someone who turns away

translated_text:
from the Quran and Sunnah to the words of someone whose agreement or disagreement with them he cannot ascertain. As for someone who opposes the Quran and Sunnah with statements that contradict them, he is like a traveller who leaves the known road to Mecca and takes the road to Cyprus, hoping to reach Mecca by it. Such is the condition of someone who abandons what is known from the Quran and Sunnah for contradictory statements made by Zayd or ‘Amr, whoever they may be. Everyone’s statements may be accepted or rejected, except those of the Messenger of Allah—Allah bless him and grant him peace. In this regard, I have witnessed astonishing things whose number is known only to the One who knows what hearts conceal.

As for the reported hadith:

“Some knowledge is like a hidden treasure: none knows it except those who have knowledge of Allah, and when they mention it, none rejects it except those who are heedless concerning Allah.”

Shaykh al-Islam Abū Ismā‘īl al-Ansārī narrated it in his book entitled The Distinction between Those Who Affirm the Divine Attributes and Those Who Negate Them. In it, he included reports concerning the divine attributes: authentic and singular reports, reports with connected and disconnected chains, and reports stopping at the Companions. Abū Hāmid al-Ghazālī also mentioned it in his books. The latter interprets it in a manner consistent with his own statements, in which he inclines towards views resembling those of the philosophers and others who deny the divine attributes.

 قَدْ حَمَلَهُ أَبُو الْوَلِيدِ بْنُ رُشْدٍ الْحَفِيدُ الْفَيْلَسُوفُ وَأَمْثَالُهُ عَلَى عُلُومِ الْبَاطِنِيَّةِ
translated_text:
“What is meant by this is the hadiths concerning the divine attributes.” Thus, he interpreted it according to the views of those who affirm the divine attributes, in opposition to Abū Hāmid’s view.

The hadith’s chain of transmission is not established, as the experts agree, and it is not related in the principal authoritative hadith collections. There is therefore no need to discuss its interpretation. Even supposing that the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—said it, its meaning is unspecified: it identifies no particular position. Hence, whenever someone claims that it refers to his own position, his opponent can make the same claim.

There is no doubt that the view of Yahyā ibn ‘Ammār, Abū Ismā‘īl al-Ansārī, and others who affirm the divine attributes is closer to the truth than that of those who deny them, since this knowledge is, by common agreement, part of the knowledge of the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—and of the Companions. It is well known that no one transmits the position of those who deny the attributes from the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—or his Companions, whether through an authentic or a weak chain. The position of those who affirm the attributes is quite otherwise: the Quran, the hadiths, and the reports from the Companions are full of it. How, then, can the Prophet’s words—Allah bless him and grant him peace—be understood as referring to knowledge that no one has transmitted from him, rather than to the knowledge transmitted from him and his Companions?

Likewise, al-Bukhārī related that ‘Alī—may Allah be pleased with him—said:

“Tell people what they can understand, and leave aside what they would reject. Would you like Allah and His Messenger to be disbelieved?”

Abū al-Walīd ibn Rushd the grandson, the philosopher, and others like him have interpreted this as referring to the teachings of the esotericists

original_text:

" مَا مِنْ رَجُلٍ يُحَدِّثُ قَوْمًا حَدِيثًا لَا تَبْلُغُهُ عُقُولُهُمْ إلَّا كَانَ فِتْنَةً لِبَعْضِهِمْ "

translated_text:
—the philosophers who deny the divine attributes. This is an obvious distortion, for ‘Alī’s words, “Would you like Allah and His Messenger to be disbelieved?” indicate that this concerns something the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—conveyed. Yet no Muslim has transmitted anything from the Prophet—Allah bless him and grant him peace—in support of the views of those who deny the attributes among the philosophers, Jahmiyyah, Qarāmitah, and Mu‘tazilah, through either an authentic or a weak chain. How, then, could Allah and His Messenger be disbelieved concerning something that no one has transmitted from Allah and His Messenger? By contrast, those who affirm the attributes have transmitted numerous, well-known hadiths describing the Lord’s attributes, His angels, His Paradise, and His Fire. These may be beyond some people’s understanding, so relating them may give rise to the fear that Allah and His Messenger will be disbelieved.

Of the same kind are the words of ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd:

“No man relates to people something beyond their understanding without its becoming a trial for some of them.”

In his statements, whether relating something or giving instructions, Ibn Mas‘ūd was among the most emphatic in affirming the attributes and among the most prolific transmitters of the hadiths concerning them. His students were among the most eminent of the Successors and the most emphatic in this regard. The same applies to the students of Ibn ‘Abbās. The more knowledgeable a Companion was, the more emphatically he and his students affirmed the attributes.

It is thus clear that the Companions did not inwardly conceal the opposite of what they outwardly professed. They did not outwardly affirm the attributes while inwardly denying them, nor outwardly affirm a command while inwardly holding its fulfilment to be impossible. Rather, they were the most steadfast in believing what the Messenger conveyed and obeying what he commanded. This is a broad subject, encompassing matters for which there is not enough space here

to discuss them in detail. Yet we know the central principle: every utterance and deed necessarily has an outward and an inward aspect. The outward aspect of an utterance is what the tongue pronounces; its inward aspect is the realities and meanings present in the heart. The outward aspect of a deed is the movement of the body; its inward aspect is its underlying realities and the person’s intentions within the heart. Thus, when the hypocrite outwardly conformed to Islam without possessing the realities of faith, this did not benefit him, and he was among the losers. Indeed, he was in the lowest depths of the Fire. Allah Most High says:

“Among the people are some who say, ‘We believe in Allah and the Last Day,’ but they are not believers.”

“They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive only themselves, though they do not realize it.”

And the subsequent verses. At the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah, Allah revealed four verses describing the believers, two describing the disbelievers, and more than ten describing the hypocrites. Allah Most High also says:

“When the hypocrites come to you, they say, ‘We testify that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah.’ Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger, and Allah testifies that the hypocrites are liars.”

And the rest of the surah. Allah Most High also says:

“Do not let those who hasten into disbelief grieve you—those who say with their mouths, ‘We believe,’ while their hearts do not believe.”

To the end of the verse.

The heretics outwardly profess agreement with the Muslims while inwardly concealing the opposite. They are worse than the hypocrites, for hypocrites are of two kinds: one kind outwardly professes faith while inwardly concealing disbelief, without claiming that the disbelief concealed within is the true reality of faith. The heretics, however, claim that the disbelief they conceal within is the true reality of faith

 هَذَا قَالُوهُ عَلَى سَبِيلِ التَّقِيَّةِ ثُمَّ فَتَحُوا بَابَ النِّفَاقِ لِلْقَرَامِطَةِ الْبَاطِنِيَّةِ
translated_text:
and that the prophets and Allah’s allies are of their kind, concealing the same disbelief and theological negation that they themselves conceal. Thus, they combine concealing disbelief with claiming that this concealed belief is true faith according to those possessed of spiritual knowledge. They do not disclose to those who respond to them that what is concealed impugns the Messenger and the believers and declares him a liar. Rather, they present it as part of the Messenger’s perfection and the completeness of his spiritual state. They claim that what he did represents the utmost perfection, something only the most perfect of men can accomplish: governing people justly and developing the world along a virtuous path. Some groups may regard this as true both inwardly and outwardly. Their position thus ultimately makes hypocrisy the very reality of faith, although it is necessarily known that hypocrisy is the opposite of faith.

For this reason, their principal gateway has been Shiism and the Rāfidī doctrine, for the Rāfidīs are the most ignorant and mendacious of the sects, and the furthest removed from understanding transmitted sources and rational matters. They make dissimulation one of the foundations of their religion and attribute countless lies to the Prophet’s household—so many that only Allah can enumerate them. They even report that Jaʿfar al-Sādiq said, “Dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my forefathers.”

“Dissimulation” is the hallmark of hypocrisy, for its reality according to them is to say with their tongues what is not in their hearts—and this is the very reality of hypocrisy.

Since this is one of the foundations of their religion, whenever transmitters report anything from ʿAlī or another member of the Prophet’s household that agrees with Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah, they say, “They said this by way of dissimulation.” They then opened the door of hypocrisy to the Qarmatian esotericists

—the philosophers among the Ismāʿīlīs, the Nusayrīs, and others like them. They treated the Messenger’s words as belonging to this same category: he outwardly expressed the opposite of what he inwardly concealed, and privately confided the opposite of what he publicly proclaimed. In effect, their position made the Messenger the leader of the hypocrites. Yet he—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is the truthful and trustworthy one, who explains to people what has been sent down to them, conveys his Lord’s message, and addresses them in clear Arabic.

Allah Most High says:

“We have not sent any messenger except in the language of his people, so that he might make things clear to them.”

And He says:

“We have made it an Arabic Quran so that you may understand.”

And He says:

“We have certainly made the Quran easy for remembrance. Is there anyone who will take heed?”

And He says:

“We have made it easy in your language only so that you may give glad tidings through it to the righteous and warn a contentious people.”

And He says:

“The tongue of the one to whom they allude is foreign, whereas this is clear Arabic.”

And He says:

“We have sent down to you the Reminder so that you may explain to people what has been sent down to them.”

And He says:

“It is for Us to gather it and recite it.”

“So when We have recited it, follow its recitation.”

“Then it is for Us to explain it.”

And He says:

“This is a blessed Book which We have sent down to you, so that they may reflect upon its verses and those of understanding may take heed.”

And He says:

“Do they not reflect upon the Quran, or are there locks upon their hearts?”

And He says:

“Are the messengers responsible for anything but conveying the message clearly?”

And the messengers said:

“Our Lord knows that we have indeed been sent to you. Our duty is only to convey the message clearly.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘Obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, he is responsible only for what he has been charged with, and you are responsible for what you have been charged with. If you obey him, you will be guided. And the Messenger’s duty is only

to convey the message clearly.’”

And Allah Most High says:

“Obey Allah and obey the Messenger. But if you turn away, Our Messenger’s duty is only to convey the message clearly.”

And He says:

“O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not conveyed His message.”

These and similar passages make clear that the messengers are required to convey the message clearly. The verbs bāna, abāna, istabāna, tabayyana, and bayyana can all be used intransitively to mean that something has become clear. One may also use abāna and bayyana to mean that someone else made it clear, and tabayyana and istabāna to mean that someone discerned it. It is well known that the messengers fulfilled their duty. Indeed, Allah took a covenant from the people of knowledge that they would explain that knowledge and not conceal it, and He condemned those who conceal it. Allah Most High says:

“And when Allah took a covenant from those who were given the Scripture: ‘You must make it clear to people and not conceal it.’”

And He says:

Indeed, many groups ultimately came to witness the reality of divine decree in creation, and imagined that whoever witnessed it was no longer subject to commands and prohibitions, or to the promise of reward and the threat of punishment. This is the religion of the polytheists who said:

translated_text:
And these people are worse than the Qadarī Muʿtazilites, who acknowledge commands and prohibitions, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment, but deny divine decree. The latter resemble the Magians, whereas the former resemble the polytheists who reject the prophets and revealed laws. They are thus among the worst of people. These matters have been discussed at length elsewhere.

“The point here” is that the outward must have an inward reality that gives it substance, confirms it, and accords with it. Whoever observes the outward forms of religion without inward belief is a hypocrite, while whoever claims an inward reality that contradicts its outward forms is a disbeliever and a hypocrite. Rather, the inward reality of religion gives substance to its outward forms, confirms them, and accords with them; its outward forms likewise accord with its inward reality, confirm it, and give it substance. Just as a human being must have both a soul and a body that are in harmony, a person’s religion must have outward and inward aspects that are in harmony. The inward aspect pertains to a person’s inner self, and the outward aspect to their outward self.

The Quran is full of statements concerning the inward and outward aspects of religion, and the inward is the foundation of the outward. As Abū Hurayrah said:

“The heart is king, and the bodily members are its troops. If the king is good, its troops are good; if the king is corrupt, its troops are corrupt.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh: if it is sound, the rest of the body is sound because of it; if it is corrupt, the rest of the body is corrupt because of it. Indeed, it is the heart.”

It is also reported in the Musnad that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Islam is outwardly manifest, while faith is in the heart.”

And Allah Most High said:

“Those are the ones in whose hearts He has inscribed

faith and strengthened them with a spirit from Him.”

Allah Most High also said:

“It is He who sent down tranquillity into the hearts of the believers so that they might grow still further in faith.”

And He said:

“Whomever Allah wills to guide, He opens his breast to Islam; and whomever He wills to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted, as though he were ascending into the sky.”

And He said:

“Allah has sent down the finest speech: a Book consistent in its parts and reiterating its teachings. The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver at it; then their skins and hearts soften at the remembrance of Allah.”

And He said:

“The believers are only those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned, whose faith increases when His verses are recited to them, and who put their trust in their Lord.”

And He said:

“Those who believe and whose hearts find reassurance in the remembrance of Allah—surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find reassurance.”

There are many similar passages in the Quran.

Concerning the disbelievers, He said:

“Those are the ones whose hearts Allah does not will to purify.”

And He said:

“Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering.”

There are other similar passages.

We therefore ask Allah the Magnificent, by His grace and generosity, to set right our inward and outward selves and to guide us to what He loves and is pleased with in all our affairs. All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless our master Muhammad, his family, and his Companions, and grant them abundant peace.

The “first” is the hardened heart: rigid and dry, like a stone that takes no impression. Faith is not inscribed within it, nor is knowledge imprinted upon it, for that requires a soft, receptive place. The “second” must be one of two kinds: either the truth is firmly established within it and does not depart, owing to its strength together with its tenderness, or its tenderness is accompanied by weakness and laxity. The latter is the diseased heart, while the former is both strong and tender.

The heart resembles the limbs of the body—the hand, for example. A hand may be rigid and dry, unable to bend or grasp, or grasping only with violence: this resembles the hardened heart. Or it may be weak and diseased, rendered incapable by its weakness and disease: this resembles the diseased heart. Or it may grasp with strength and suppleness: this resembles the knowledgeable, merciful heart. Through mercy, it is free of hardness; through knowledge, it is free of disease, for this disease arises from doubts and misconceptions. Hence, those unlike these are described as possessing knowledge, faith, and humble submission.

translated_text:
have risen above the level of faith—as some speculative theologians imagine. Rather, they possess both knowledge and faith, as Allah Most High says:

“But those among them firmly grounded in knowledge, and the believers, believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you.”

And He says:

“Those who were given knowledge and faith will say, ‘You have indeed remained, according to Allah’s decree…’”

Thus, His words:

“Those firmly grounded in knowledge say, ‘We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord,’”

parallel this verse. Here He states that those given knowledge know that it is the truth from their Lord, while there He states that they say concerning the ambiguous passages: “We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.” Both passages concern matters that give rise to doubt and confusion for others. There, the discussion concerns ambiguous passages; here, it concerns what Satan casts forth, which Allah annuls, after which Allah makes His verses firm. Here He contrasts what is firmly established with what Allah has annulled of what Satan cast forth.

For this reason, some early Quran commentators said that the “definitive” is the abrogating, and the “ambiguous” is the abrogated. They meant—and Allah knows best—His words:

“Allah annuls what Satan casts forth; then Allah makes His verses firm.”

Abrogation here means removing what Satan has cast forth, not repealing what Allah has legislated.

I have pointed out the reason for this in a later passage, namely: Allah sometimes contrasts the definitive with the ambiguous, and at other times with the abrogated. In the broad terminology of the early generations, “the abrogated” includes any text whose apparent meaning is set aside because of stronger countervailing evidence, such as restricting the scope of a general expression or qualifying an unrestricted one. Such a text is ambiguous because it admits of two meanings

and this includes expressions requiring clarification, for these too are ambiguous. Making them definitive means ruling out any unintended meaning that might be imagined in them. The same applies to a text whose ruling has been repealed, for all of this involves annulling what Satan casts into the interpretation of the Quran.

For this reason, they used to ask: “Do you know the abrogating from the abrogated?” Once the abrogating is known, the definitive is known. Accordingly, it is valid to speak of “the definitive and the abrogated,” just as one speaks of “the definitive and the ambiguous.”

His subsequent words,

“Then Allah makes His verses firm,”

establish that all the verses are made firm, both their definitive and their ambiguous passages, as He says:

“Alif Lām Rā.”

“A Book whose verses have been made firm, then set out in detail.”

And He says:

“These are the verses of the firmly established Book,”

according to one of the two interpretations.

Elsewhere, He divides the verses into two categories, definitive and ambiguous, as He says:

“In it are definitive verses, which are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous.”

These ambiguous passages are among what the Most Merciful revealed, not among what Satan cast forth and Allah annulled. Thus, in the Quran, the definitive is sometimes contrasted with the ambiguous, both being among Allah’s verses; at other times, it is contrasted with what Allah annulled of what Satan cast forth.

Some people contrast it with whatever Allah has abrogated, without qualification, even saying: “This verse is definitive, not abrogated.” They regard what is abrogated as not definitive, even though Allah originally revealed it, following the apparent sense of His words:

“Allah annuls,”

“Then Allah makes His verses firm.”

These, then, are three meanings contrasted with the definitive that should be borne in mind. In summary, “making firm” sometimes concerns revelation itself, in which case it is contrasted with what Satan casts forth. The definitive is what has been revealed from Allah and made firm by Him: He has distinguished it from anything with which it might be confused and separated from it whatever does not belong to it. For making something firm involves separation, distinction, differentiation, and delimitation, through which its identity is established and it is perfected. Hence its meaning includes prevention, just as delimitation does; prevention is part of its meaning, not its entire meaning.

At other times, “making firm” concerns keeping the revelation in force, according to those who contrast it with abrogation in the sense of repealing what has been prescribed. This is a technical usage. Alternatively—and this more closely accords with the usage of the early generations—it may be said that they called every removal “abrogation,” whether the removal of a ruling or of an apparent meaning.

What Satan casts into a person’s recitation may affect the very words of the one conveying it, what he hears, or his understanding, as Allah says:

“He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their capacity”—to the end of the verse.

It is well known that when someone hears a text whose ruling, or one of whose implications, has been set aside, Satan casts into that recitation the suggestion that he should follow what has been abrogated. Allah then makes His verses firm through the abrogating text, by which the ruling is repealed and the intended meaning clarified.

On this understanding, it is valid to say: “The ambiguous is the abrogated,” in this respect. And Allah knows best.

At other times, “making firm” concerns interpretation and meaning: it consists in distinguishing the reality

In contrast to the definitive verses are the ambiguous verses, which resemble both one thing and another and thus admit either meaning. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: “The definitive is that in which there is no discrepancy; the ambiguous is that which appears in one form in one passage and in another form elsewhere.”

Allah did not say of the ambiguous verses that no one knows their explanation and meaning except Him. Rather, He said:

“But no one knows its ta’wīl (interpretation) except Allah.”

This decisively settles the dispute between those who disagree on this matter, for Allah has stated that no one knows its ta’wīl except Him. Pausing at this point in the recitation is supported by much evidence and is the position held by the Companions of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the majority of the Successors, and the overwhelming majority of the Muslim community.

Yet He did not deny their knowledge of its meaning and explanation. Rather, He said:

“A blessed Book which We have revealed to you, that they might reflect upon its verses.”

This includes both the definitive and the ambiguous verses. Something whose meaning cannot be understood cannot be reflected upon. He also said:

“Do they not reflect upon the Quran?”

He did not exclude any part of it by forbidding reflection upon it. Allah and His Messenger condemned only those who pursue the ambiguous, seeking discord and seeking its ta’wīl. As for those who reflect upon both the definitive and the ambiguous, as Allah has commanded, seeking to understand them and know their meaning, Allah has not condemned them. Rather, He has commanded this and commended it.

translated_text:
sought to interpret the letters of the alphabet at the beginnings of the surahs as indicating how long this community would endure. Some in later times followed the same approach, agreeing with the Sabean astrologers. They claimed that it would endure for 693 years, this being the numerical value of those letters in the abjad system after repeated letters are excluded. This is a form of ta’wīl concerning the events of the Last Day foretold by the Quran.

It is also reported that some of the Christians who came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, with the delegation from Najrān interpreted “Indeed, We” and “We” as meaning that there are three gods, because the pronoun is plural. This is a ta’wīl concerning belief in Allah. Thus, the former offered a ta’wīl concerning the Last Day, while the latter offered a ta’wīl concerning Allah.

It is well known that “Indeed, We” and “We” are among the ambiguous expressions. They may refer to one individual accompanied by others of the same kind, or to one individual accompanied by his helpers, even if they are not of the same kind. They may also refer to one individual magnifying himself, who stands in the place of someone accompanied by others because of the multiplicity of his names, each name taking the place of a named entity. Such an expression is therefore ambiguous: its wording is one, but its meanings are diverse.

“Equivocal terms” are among the ambiguous expressions, as are some “univocal terms.” Quranic commentators call these “multiple senses and parallel usages,” and have compiled “Books of Multiple Senses and Parallel Usages.” Multiple senses concern equivocal terms, while parallel usages concern univocal terms. Some of our companions who have written on this subject have supposed that the multiple senses

and parallel usages both concern equivocal terms: they are parallel with regard to wording and have multiple senses with regard to meaning. Yet the matter is not as he claims. Rather, anyone who examines their words carefully will find that they explicitly support what we have said.

Those in whose hearts is deviation abandon the unambiguous passages, in which there is no uncertainty, such as:

“Your God is one God.”

“Indeed, I am Allah. There is no deity except Me, so worship Me.”

“Allah has not taken a son, nor is there any deity alongside Him.”

“He has not taken a son and has no partner in His dominion.”

“He neither begets nor is born.”

“Nor is anyone comparable to Him.”

Instead, they follow the ambiguous passages, seeking to cause discord—to lead people astray by applying them where they do not belong—and seeking their ta’wīl, meaning the reality of what they speak of.

This is because “speech is of two kinds”: non-declarative speech, which includes commands, and declarative speech. The ta’wīl of a command is the very act commanded. Thus, some of the early generations said that the Sunnah is the ta’wīl of the command.

‘Ā’ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, used to say when bowing and prostrating: ‘Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me.’ He was thereby putting the Quran into practice.”

She meant His words:

“Then glorify your Lord with praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.”

As for declarative speech, its ta’wīl is the very thing reported, when it comes to pass; its ta’wīl is not the understanding of its meaning.

The term “ta’wīl” occurs in several places in the Quran with this meaning. Allah Most High says:

“We have certainly brought them a Book which We have explained in detail with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for people who believe.”

“Do they await anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes, those who had forgotten it before will say, ‘The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth.’”

He thus states that He has explained the Book in detail: this means clarifying it and distinguishing its meanings so that no confusion remains. He then says, “Do they await”—that is, wait for—“anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes,” and so on to the end of the verse.

This refers precisely to the coming to pass of what the Quran foretells concerning the Resurrection and its signs: the Beast, Gog and Magog, the sun rising from the west, the coming of your Lord and the angels, rank upon rank, and what the Hereafter contains of records of deeds, scales, Paradise, Hell, the various forms of bliss and punishment, and other things. At that time they will say:

“The messengers of our Lord certainly came with the truth. Have we any intercessors who will intercede for us? Or could we be sent back, so that we might act differently from the way we used to act?”

None but Allah knows the timing, extent, and nature of these matters foretold by the Quran. For Allah says:

“No soul knows what delights have been kept hidden for them.”

And He says:

“I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived.”

Ibn ‘Abbās said: “Nothing of what is in Paradise exists in this world except the names.” Allah has told us that Paradise contains wine, milk, water, silk, gold, silver, and other things, and we know with certainty that

the reality of those things is not identical to that of their worldly counterparts. Rather, there is a tremendous difference between them despite their resemblance, as in His words:

“And they will be given it in a similar form.”

According to one of the two interpretations, it resembles what is in this world without being identical to it. Thus, the names of those realities resemble the names of these realities, just as the realities themselves resemble one another in certain respects. When those names are used in addressing us, we understand them through what the two have in common. Yet those realities have a distinctive nature that we cannot apprehend in this world. We have no means of apprehending it, since we have experienced neither those realities themselves nor anything resembling them in every respect. Those realities, as they truly are, constitute the fulfilment of what Allah has told us.

This also refutes the Jews, Christians, and Sabians, whether philosophers or others, who deny that there is eating, drinking, clothing, or sexual intercourse in Paradise, and reject the existence of what the Quran describes. Someone who enters Islam but acts hypocritically toward the believers interprets these descriptions as parables intended to convey spiritual bliss, if he belongs to the Sabian philosophers who deny bodily resurrection. If he belongs to the hypocrites of the two faiths who affirm bodily resurrection, he interprets them as conveying the bliss of Paradise consisting of spiritual enjoyment, pleasing sounds, and fragrant scents. Thus, every misguided person distorts words from their proper meanings to conform to what he believes to be real.

In doing so, he also follows what is ambiguous: the names resemble one another, and the things named resemble one another, yet their differences are greater than their similarities. Thus these people follow this

ambiguity, “seeking discord” through the specious arguments they advance to show that these realities cannot exist in Paradise, and “seeking its interpretation” so as to reduce it to what they know and are familiar with in this world.

Allah Most High says:

“And none knows its fulfilment except Allah.”

For Allah has said concerning those realities:

“No soul knows what joy has been kept hidden for them.”

Neither an angel brought near nor a prophet sent knows it.

In His words, “And none knows its fulfilment,” the pronoun may refer either to the Book or to what is ambiguous. If it refers to the Book, as in His expressions “of it” and “of it”—“They follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation”—this is valid. For, regarding all the verses of the Book, both clear and ambiguous, that tell of the unseen in which we have been commanded to believe, Allah alone knows the true nature of that unseen and when it will occur.

This may be supported by the fact that Allah attributes fulfilment to the entire Book, while stating that it has been explained in detail, in His words:

“We have certainly brought them a Book which We have explained in detail with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for people who believe.”

“Are they waiting for anything but its fulfilment? On the Day its fulfilment comes…”

Thus, He attributes the coming fulfilment to the Book that has been explained in detail.

We have already explained that Allah alone knows the time, extent, kind, and true nature of that fulfilment. We know only some of its attributes, within the limits of our knowledge, since we have nothing comparable to it in our experience. Likewise, He says:

“Rather, they have denied that which they have not encompassed in knowledge and whose fulfilment has not yet come to them.”

translated_text:
And if fulfilment pertains to the whole Book and means what we have described, the difficulty is removed, and this becomes comparable to His words:

“They ask you about the Hour: when will it arrive? Say, ‘Knowledge of it rests only with my Lord. None but He will reveal it at its appointed time. It weighs heavily upon the heavens and the earth.’”

Up to His words:

“Knowledge of it rests only with Allah.”

Likewise, He says:

“People ask you about the Hour. Say, ‘Knowledge of it rests only with Allah.’ And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.”

He thus states that knowledge of it rests only with Allah. This means knowledge of its precise time and true nature; otherwise, we already know those attributes of it that He has told us about. Knowledge of the Book’s fulfilment is therefore like knowledge of the Hour, and the Hour is itself part of its fulfilment. This is clear and evident. That knowledge of the Hour rests with Allah does not preclude our knowing what we know of its attributes and circumstances, or our explaining the texts that describe its circumstances. The same applies here.

If, however, the pronoun refers to what is ambiguous, as many people maintain, this is because the promised rewards and threatened punishments described in the reports are ambiguous, unlike commands and prohibitions. Hence the words found in transmitted reports:

“Acting upon what is clear in it and believing in what is ambiguous in it.”

For the purpose of a report is that it should be believed. The promised rewards and threatened punishments described in such reports contain the ambiguity we have mentioned, unlike commands and prohibitions.

Hence some scholars have said that “the ambiguous” comprises parables, promises and warnings, while “the clear” comprises commands and prohibitions. The latter are distinct and not confused with anything else: they concern things we do, which we know through actual experience, and things we refrain from doing, which we must necessarily be able to conceive.

Another occurrence of the term ta’wīl (fulfilment) in the Quran is in His words, Exalted is He:

“Rather, they have denied what they have not fully comprehended and whose fulfilment has not yet come to them.”

The pronoun refers to the Quran, or to “what they have not fully comprehended,” which itself refers to the Quran. He, Exalted is He, says:

“This Quran could not have been fabricated by anyone other than Allah. Rather, it is a confirmation of what came before it and a detailed exposition of the Book, in which there is no doubt, from the Lord of all worlds.

“Or do they say, ‘He fabricated it’? Say, ‘Then produce a surah like it, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful.’

“The key point here” is that the meaning of an account has a mental representation that exists within the knower—in the human mind, for example—while that meaning also has an established reality outside the mind. The wording initially signifies the meaning in the mind, then serves as an intermediary for it or signifies the external reality. Its fulfilment is thus the external reality, whereas knowing its explanation and meaning is knowing the mental representation.

translated_text:
their proper places.

Error predominates in both groups. The former fall short in understanding the Quran, resembling those of whom it was said:

“Among them are unlettered people who know the Scripture only through mere recitation.”

The latter transgress, resembling those who displace words from their proper places.

Some later scholars framed the issue using an offensive label, saying:

“Allah cannot speak without intending any meaning, contrary to the Hashwiyyah.”

Yet no Muslim has ever said that Allah speaks words devoid of meaning. The dispute is only whether He speaks words whose meaning is not understood. There is a vast difference between denying that the speaker intends a meaning and denying that the person addressed understands it.

He then advanced an argument inconsistent with his own principles, saying:

“This would be purposeless, and purposelessness is impossible for Allah.”

Yet he holds that nothing Allah does is in any way reprehensible and that He may do anything. Nor can he say, “Purposelessness is an imperfection and is therefore excluded from Him,” because the dispute concerns letters, which, in his view, are created and belong to the category of acts. According to him, an act may possess any quality whatsoever. Thus, his position rests on neither authentic transmitted evidence nor clear reason.

The source of discord between the two groups, and the point at which their minds become bewildered, is that those claiming to provide ta’wīl erred both in asserting that the scholars know the ta’wīl and in claiming that ta’wīl means their own interpretation, which is a displacement of words from their proper places. The confusion arises from the different meanings of the term ta’wīl. In the usage of later jurists, speculative theologians, hadith scholars, Sufis, and others, “ta’wīl” means diverting an expression from its more likely meaning to a less likely meaning on the strength of accompanying evidence. This is the ta’wīl they discuss in the principles of jurisprudence and in disputed questions.

When one of them says, “This hadith, or this text, is subject to ta’wīl,” or, “It is to be understood in such-and-such a sense,” another replies, “This is a form of ta’wīl, and ta’wīl requires evidence.” The person advancing such an interpretation has two obligations: to show that the wording admits the meaning he claims, and to establish the evidence that requires departing from the apparent meaning in favour of that meaning.

This is the ta’wīl over which they dispute in matters concerning Allah’s attributes: one writes to refute or condemn ta’wīl; another says, “The verses concerning the attributes must not be reinterpreted”; another says, “Rather, they must be reinterpreted”; and a third says, “Rather, ta’wīl is permissible: it is employed when doing so serves a benefit and omitted when refraining serves a benefit,” or, “It is appropriate for scholars, but not for others.” There are other such statements and disputes.

As for “ta’wīl” in the usage of the early generations, it has two meanings. The first is explaining speech and clarifying its meaning, whether this agrees with its apparent meaning or differs from it. Thus, in their usage, ta’wīl and tafsīr (exegesis) are close in meaning or synonymous.

And this—Allah knows best—is what Mujāhid meant when he said that the scholars know its ta’wīl. Muhammad ibn Jarīr al-Tabarī says in his Quran commentary, “Discussion of the ta’wīl of His words, such-and-such,” and, “The scholars of ta’wīl differed concerning this verse,” and similar expressions. What he means is explanation.

The “second meaning” in the usage of the early generations—which is the third sense of ta’wīl overall—is the very thing intended by the speech. If the speech is a request, its ta’wīl is the requested action itself; if it is a statement, its ta’wīl is the very thing being stated. There is a considerable difference between this meaning and the preceding one. In the preceding sense, ta’wīl belongs to the realm of knowledge and discourse, like explanation, commentary, and clarification. It exists in the mind and on the tongue, having mental, verbal, and written existence. In this sense, however, ta’wīl consists of the actual things that exist in external reality, whether past or future.

Thus, when someone says, “The sun has risen,” the ta’wīl of this is its actual rising. Here, “ta’wīl” belongs to the realm of concrete, external existence. The ta’wīl of speech, then, consists of the realities that exist externally, with their actual attributes, affairs, and conditions. Those realities cannot be known as they truly are through speech and reports alone, unless the listener has already formed a conception of them, or of something comparable to them, through something other than speech and reports. Nevertheless, he comes to know of their attributes and conditions to the extent that the speaker has conveyed them to him: whether by drawing

analogies, by offering an approximation, by referring to what they share with other things, or by other means. This third sense and established usage is that of the language in which the Quran was revealed. We have already explained this.

Examples include Jacob’s words to Joseph, peace be upon him:

“Thus will your Lord choose you, teach you the interpretation of dreams, and perfect His favour upon you.”

And His words:

“Two young men entered the prison with him. One of them said, ‘I saw myself pressing wine.’ The other said, ‘I saw myself carrying bread on my head, from which birds were eating. Tell us its interpretation, for we see that you are among those who do good.’”

“He said, ‘No food provided for you will come to you without my telling you its interpretation before it comes to you.’”

And the words of the chiefs:

“Confused dreams! We have no knowledge of the interpretation of dreams.”

“The one of the two who had been saved, remembering after a time, said, ‘I will tell you its interpretation, so send me.’”

And Joseph’s words when his family came to him in Egypt:

“He took his parents into his embrace and said, ‘Enter Egypt, Allah willing, in safety.’”

“He raised his parents onto the throne, and they fell down before him in prostration. He said, ‘My father, this is the fulfilment of my earlier dream. My Lord has made it come true.’”

Thus, the ta’wīl of dreams seen in sleep is the very reality they signify and in which they find their fulfilment, as Joseph said:

“This is the fulfilment of my earlier dream.”

The one who knows their ta’wīl is the one who tells of that reality. As Joseph said:

“No food provided for you will come to you”—meaning in a dream—“without my telling you its interpretation before it comes to you”—meaning before its fulfilment comes to you.

Allah Most High also says:

“If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

They explained this as meaning: best in its consequences and final outcome. Here, ta’wīl is the outcome of their action—referring matters to the Book and the Sunnah. In Sūrat Yūsuf, ta’wīl concerns accounts of dreams; in al-A‘rāf and Yūnus, it concerns the Quran, as it does in Sūrat Āl ‘Imrān.

In the account of Moses and the learned man, Allah Most High says:

“He said, ‘This is the parting between you and me. I will tell you the explanation of what you could not bear patiently.’”

The passage continues to His words:

“‘I did not do it of my own accord. That is the explanation of what you could not bear patiently.’”

Here, ta’wīl concerns the actions performed by the learned man: damaging the ship without its owner’s permission, killing the boy, and restoring the wall. It is thus the ta’wīl of an action, not of a statement. This is because ta’wīl is the verbal noun of awwalahu–yu’awwiluhu, just as tahwīl is the verbal noun of hawwala, and ta‘wīl that of ‘awwala. Awwala–yu’awwilu is the transitive form of āla–ya’ūlu–awlan, like hāla–yahūlu–hawlan.

The expression āla–ya’ūlu means to return or revert to something. From this comes ma’āl, meaning that to which something ultimately returns. Related to it through “greater derivation” is maw’il, for the latter comes from wa’ala, whereas the former comes from awila.

Maw’il means a place of return. Allah Most High says:

“They will find no refuge apart from Him.”
