return to him. Hence, this term is used only of someone of great standing: the person to whom the āl are attributed must be greater than they are, someone to whom they may fittingly return—as with the āl of Abraham, the āl of Lot, and the āl of Pharaoh. This is unlike ahl (family).

Awwal (first) follows the af‘al pattern, for its feminine is ūlā, as in Jumādā al-Ūlā. In Sūrat al-Qasas, Allah says:

“To Him belongs all praise in this life and the Hereafter.”

Some maintain that it follows the faw‘al pattern and give its feminine as awwala. However, this requires supporting evidence from Arab usage. Indeed, its restricted declension indicates that it follows af‘al, not faw‘al, since words on the faw‘al pattern, such as kawthar and jawhar, are fully declined.

That which precedes is called awwal—and Allah knows best—because what follows it returns to it and is built upon it. It is thus the foundation and basis of what follows. The form is an elative, not an ordinary descriptive adjective: it is like akbar and kubrā (greater or greatest), and asghar and sughrā (smaller or smallest), rather than ahmar and hamrā’ (red).

Hence, people say, “I came to him the day before yesterday.” Allah says:

“A mosque founded on righteousness from the very first day.”

“And I am the first of the Muslims.”

“And do not be the first to disbelieve in it.”

When someone is described as “the first of these people,” he is the one who surpasses them in precedence. Each one refers back to whoever preceded him and relies upon him, while all of them ultimately refer back to this earliest predecessor. Whoever takes the lead in an action and is then followed as an example by those after him becomes the predecessor to whom they all refer back. The first thus has the qualities of leadership and being followed.

The word “awwal” suggests returning and reverting, yet “awwal” also suggests beginning and that with which a beginning is made—the opposite of that which returns. This is because something is first only in relation to what follows it, for one says:

translated_text:
“the first of the Muslims” and “the first day.” The sense of returning and reverting belongs to the second term of the possessive construction, not the first.

When we say “the āl of so-and-so,” however, the return is to the first term. For the elative form denotes pre-eminence in being that to which others ultimately return and refer. Its indication of pre-eminence shows that it denotes a destination and point of reference, not something that itself returns and refers elsewhere. There is no pre-eminence in something’s returning and referring to another; rather, pre-eminence lies in its being that to which others return and refer. Since the form is an elative, it indicates pre-eminence in being a destination and point of reference. Absolute pre-eminence in this respect requires that it be what precedes and comes at the beginning. And Allah knows best.

Thus, the ta’wīl of speech is that to which the speaker directs it, that to which the speech leads, or that to which the speaker takes it to refer. A verbal noun on the taf‘īl pattern may accompany a verb of a different pattern, as in His words:

“And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion.”

Here the wording is wa-tabattal ilayhi tabtīlan. It is therefore permissible to say ta’awwala al-kalāmu ilā hādhā al-ma‘nā ta’wīlan (“the speech led to this meaning”), ta’awwaltu al-kalāma ta’wīlan (“I interpreted the speech”), and awwaltu al-kalāma ta’wīlan (“I interpreted the speech”).

The verbal noun stands in place of an adjective. A verbal noun may function adjectivally with an active meaning, as in ‘adl (a just person), sawm (one who fasts), and fitr (one who is not fasting). It may also carry a passive meaning, as with darb (“striking”) in “a dirham struck by the emir,” and khalq (“creation”) in “This is Allah’s creation.”

Ta’wīl, then, is that to which speech is directed, that to which it leads, or that to which it itself comes. Speech returns and reverts, comes to rest, leads, and is directed only to its reality

which is precisely what is intended by it. This is as one of the early scholars explained His words:

“Every announcement has its appointed fulfillment.”

He said: “A reality.” For if the speech is a report, it ultimately leads and refers back to the reality being reported. Otherwise, it would have no reality, outcome, or point of reference, but would instead be false. If it is a request, it ultimately leads and refers back to the reality being sought, even if its object does not exist and has not been realized. Whenever a report is a promise or a threat, it ultimately leads to the reality sought and awaited. Thus, it is reported that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, recited this verse:

“Say: He has the power to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet, or to divide you into factions.”

He said: “It will indeed come to pass, but its fulfillment has not yet come.”

It is also reported that ʿAbd Allāh said: “Five have already come to pass: the onslaught, the inevitable punishment, the smoke, the moon, and the Romans.”

Section

As for including Allah’s names and attributes, or some of them, among the ambiguous passages whose ta’wīl is known only to Allah—or believing that these constitute the ambiguous passages whose ta’wīl Allah has reserved to Himself—each of these two views is held by groups among our companions and others. Although they are correct in much of what they say and have escaped innovations into which others have fallen, this matter must be discussed from two perspectives.

First: To anyone who says, “This belongs to the ambiguous passages, and its meaning cannot be understood,” we say: As for the evidence that this is false, I know of no one among the early generations of this community or its leading scholars—neither Ahmad ibn Hanbal nor anyone else—who classified this among the ambiguous passages

covered by this verse, denied that anyone could know its meaning, or treated Allah’s names and attributes as unintelligible foreign speech. Nor did they say that Allah sends down speech whose meaning no one understands. Rather, their statements had sound meanings.

Concerning the hadiths about the divine attributes, they said: “Let them stand as transmitted.” They forbade, rejected, and refuted the reinterpretations of the Jahmiyyah, which strip the texts of the meanings they convey. The statements of Ahmad and the imams before him clearly show that they rejected the Jahmiyyah’s reinterpretations, affirmed the texts according to the meanings they convey, and understood some of what they indicate, just as they understood the other texts concerning promises, warnings, merits, and other matters.

Ahmad also said, “Let them stand as transmitted,” concerning hadiths other than those about the divine attributes, including hadiths containing warnings, such as the Prophet’s saying:

“Whoever cheats us is not one of us.”

He also said this concerning hadiths about merits. What he meant was that the wording of a hadith must not be distorted from its proper sense, as is done by those who distort it and whose distortion is called “interpretation” in later terminology. Thus, what these later figures call interpretation is, in the imams’ judgment, false distortion.

Likewise, Ahmad explicitly stated in his book Refutation of the Heretics and the Jahmiyyah that they clung to the ambiguous passages of the Quran. Ahmad discussed those ambiguous passages and explained their meaning and interpretation in a manner contrary to the Jahmiyyah’s reinterpretation, following the path of the imams before him. This establishes the imams’ agreement that they know the meaning of these ambiguous passages and that their explanation and interpretation must not be withheld. Rather, by the imams’ agreement, they are to be explained and interpreted without distorting them from their proper sense or deviating concerning Allah’s names and verses.

What further clarifies the confusion that has arisen here is that Ahl al-Sunnah agree on rejecting the reinterpretations of the Jahmiyyah and other deviant groups who depart from the truth. “Rejected interpretation” means diverting speech from its apparent meaning to a meaning contrary to it. If it were said that this is the interpretation mentioned in the verse, and that none but Allah knows it, this would concede to the Jahmiyyah that the verse has an interpretation contrary to what it indicates, but that none but Allah knows it. This is not the position of the early generations and the imams. Rather, their position is to deny and reject these reinterpretations, not to suspend judgment about them. In their view, reading the verse or hadith is itself its explanation. Such texts are to be left as transmitted, conveying their meanings, without distortion or deviation.

The evidence that this is not ambiguous speech whose meaning cannot be known is as follows:

There is no doubt that Allah has named Himself in the Quran with names such as the Most Merciful, the Most Loving, the Almighty, the Compeller, the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the Most Compassionate, and others like these. He has described Himself with attributes such as those set forth in Surah al-Ikhlās, the Verse of the Throne, the opening of Surah al-Hadīd, and the closing of Surah al-Hashr, and in His words:

“Indeed, Allah knows all things,”

and is

“Powerful over all things.”

He says that He

“loves those who are mindful of Him,”

“those who act justly,”

and “those who do good,”

and that He is pleased with those who believe and do righteous deeds.

“So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them.”

“That is because they followed what angered Allah.”

“But Allah disliked their going forth.”

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.”

“Then He rose over the Throne. He knows what enters the earth and what emerges from it, what descends from heaven and what ascends into it. And He is with you wherever you are.”

“And He is the One who

is God in heaven and God on earth; and He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.”

“To Him ascends good speech, and righteous deeds raise it.”

“Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see.”

“And He is Allah in the heavens and on earth.”

“What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two Hands?”

“Rather, both His Hands are outstretched; He spends however He wills.”

“And the Face of your Lord, full of majesty and honour, will remain.”

“Desiring His Face.”

“So that you might be brought up under My Eye.”

And other passages like these.

Anyone who claims that these are ambiguous texts whose meaning cannot be known should be asked: Do you say this about all the names and attributes with which Allah has described Himself, or only some of them?

If you say that this applies to all of them, that is manifest obstinacy and a denial of what is necessarily known in Islam—indeed, outright disbelief. For we understand a meaning from His words:

“Indeed, Allah knows all things.”

And we understand from His words:

“Indeed, Allah is Powerful over all things,”

a meaning different from the first. We understand a meaning from His words:

“My mercy encompasses all things.”

And we understand a meaning from His words:

“Indeed, Allah is Almighty, capable of vengeance.”

Muslim children—indeed, every rational person—understand this. I have encountered someone from the Maghrib who embraced innovation and denial—despite his affiliation with hadith, corrupt philosophy had influenced him—who says: “We call Allah the Most Merciful, the All-Knowing, and the All-Powerful merely as proper names, without understanding from them any meaning indicating anything whatsoever. Likewise, concerning His words, ‘They encompass nothing of His knowledge,’ we utter this expression without saying that He possesses knowledge.” And this

This obstinate disputant should then be asked: “Do these names indicate the God who is worshipped and a reality that exists, or not?”

If he says no, he is an outright denier of God, and I know of no Muslim who says this.

If he says yes, he should be asked: “Why, then, do you understand that they indicate the Lord Himself, yet fail to understand that they indicate the meanings they contain, such as mercy and knowledge, when both are equally indicated?”

He must then say: “Yes, because the existence of attributes is rationally impossible, since it entails composition or a beginning in time, unlike the divine essence.”

He should then be addressed as the second group is addressed, as we shall explain: those who acknowledge that some of the meanings of these names and attributes can be understood, but not others.

He should be asked: “What is the difference between what you affirm and what you deny, or what you refrain from either affirming or denying?” The distinction must rest either on revelation—because one of the two texts conveys its meaning conclusively or apparently, unlike the other—or on reason, because one of the two meanings may or must be affirmed, whereas the other may not. Both grounds, however, are invalid in most cases.

As for the “first,” the Quran’s indication that He is Most Merciful, Compassionate, Loving, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, Most High and Magnificent is like its indication that He is All-Knowing and All-Powerful. There is no difference between them in terms of the text. Likewise, its mention of His mercy, love and highness is like its mention of His will and intent.

 إرَادَتُهُ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ جِنْسِ إرَادَةِ خَلْقِهِ قِيلَ لَهُ: وَرَحْمَتُهُ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ جِنْسِ رَحْمَةِ خَلْقِهِ وَكَذَلِكَ مَحَبَّتُهُ. وَإِنْ قَالَ - وَهُوَ حَقِيقَةُ قَوْلِهِ -: لَمْ أُثْبِتْ الْإِرَادَةَ وَغَيْرَهَا بِالسَّمْعِ وَإِنَّمَا أَثْبَتّ الْعِلْمَ وَالْقُدْرَةَ وَالْإِرَادَةَ بِالْعَقْلِ وَكَذَلِكَ السَّمْعُ وَالْبَصَرُ وَالْكَلَامُ عَلَى إحْدَى الطَّرِيقَتَيْنِ لِأَنَّ الْفِعْلَ دَلَّ عَلَى الْقُدْرَةِ وَالْإِحْكَامِ دَلَّ عَلَى الْعِلْمِ وَالتَّخْصِيصِ دَلَّ عَلَى الْإِرَادَةِ قِيلَ لَهُ الْجَوَابُ مِنْ ثَلَاثَةِ أَوْجُهٍ: (أَحَدُهَا: أَنَّ الْإِنْعَامَ وَالْإِحْسَانَ وَكَشْفَ الضُّرِّ دَلَّ أَيْضًا عَلَى الرَّحْمَةِ كَدَلَالَةِ التَّخْصِيصِ عَلَى الْإِرَادَةِ. وَالتَّقْرِيبُ وَالْإِدْنَاءُ وَأَنْوَاعُ التَّخْصِيصِ الَّتِي لَا تَكُونُ إلَّا مِنْ الْمُحِبِّ تَدُلُّ عَلَى الْمَحَبَّةِ أَوْ مُطْلَقُ التَّخْصِيصِ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْإِرَادَةِ. وَأَمَّا التَّخْصِيصُ بِالْإِنْعَامِ فَتَخْصِيصٌ خَاصٌّ. وَالتَّخْصِيصُ بِالتَّقْرِيبِ وَالِاصْطِفَاءِ تَقْرِيبٌ خَاصٌّ. وَمَا سَلَكَهُ فِي مَسْلَكِ الْإِرَادَةِ يَسْلُكُ فِي مِثْلِ هَذَا.

translated_text:
As for the “second,” whoever affirms some attributes while denying others should be asked: “Why, for example, have you denied the reality of His mercy and love and reduced them to His will?”

If he says, “Because mercy, as understood in our case, is a tenderness that cannot be attributed to Allah,” he should be told: “Likewise, will, as understood in our case, is an inclination that cannot be attributed to Allah.”

If he says, “His will is not of the same kind as the will of His creatures,” he should be told: “Neither is His mercy of the same kind as the mercy of His creatures, and the same applies to His love.”

If he says—and this is what his position really amounts to—“I did not establish will and the other attributes through revelation. Rather, I established knowledge, power and will through reason, as well as hearing, sight and speech according to one of the two approaches, because action indicates power, precision indicates knowledge, and particularization indicates will,” he should be told that there are three answers:

(First: The bestowal of blessings, beneficence and the removal of harm also indicate mercy, just as particularization indicates will. Bringing near, drawing close, and the kinds of particularization that proceed only from one who loves indicate love. Or, particularization in general indicates will. Particularization through the bestowal of blessings, however, is a specific kind of particularization, and particularization through bringing near and choosing is a specific kind of bringing near. The same reasoning he followed to establish will applies to matters such as these.

Second: He should be told: Grant that reason does not indicate this; it can nevertheless deny it only through the same reasoning by which it would deny will. Revelation is an independent proof in its own right; indeed,

it affords greater assurance in these difficult matters, and its evidence is more conclusive. Why, then, have you denied what it indicates, or suspended judgment, and reduced all these attributes to will, when the scriptural texts make no such distinction? Whatever argument he offers can be countered with a similar argument against his affirmation of will as something additional to the act itself.

Third: He should be told: If a Jahmī says to you, “Will means nothing but the absence of coercion, or the act itself and the command to perform it,” and claims that affirming a will entails an unacceptable consequence if it is held to be beginningless, and another if it is held to have come into being—here the Muʿtazilah fell into confusion. They do not affirm a beginningless will, since they regard a beginningless attribute as impossible; nor do they affirm that a new attribute arises in Him, since most of them regard temporal occurrences inhering in Him as impossible, despite their own inconsistencies.

They therefore split into two groups:

The Baghdad school, whose innovations concerning the divine attributes and divine decree were more extreme, denied the reality of will. Al-Jāhiz said that it means nothing but the absence of coercion. Al-Kaʿbī said that it means only the act itself when it relates to His own action, and only the command itself when it relates to His servants’ obedience.

The Basran school, including Abū ʿAlī and Abū Hāshim, said: “A will comes into being without inhering in a subject; thus there is no will.” They thereby committed themselves to something coming into being without being willed, and to an attribute subsisting without a subject,

translated_text:
and both are self-evidently unsound to all rational people. His reply would be that affirming the attributes his opponent declares impossible is not impossible at all, and that both scripture and reason attest to them. If his opponent then begins disputing what scripture or reason indicates, he brands him a sophist or a Qarmatian. Yet precisely the same applies to mercy and love, for his opponents contest whether revelation and reason provide conclusive evidence for them.

His opponents should then be asked:

“By what have you established that He is All-Knowing and All-Powerful?”

Whatever evidence from revelation and reason they use to establish this also establishes will. Whatever specious objections they raise against it can be met with similar objections against His being All-Knowing and All-Powerful. When the discussion reaches the affirmation of real qualities and the claim that these entail temporal origination, or composition and dependence, the answer is what we have established elsewhere: this entails neither temporal origination nor any composition necessitating dependence upon something other than Him.

They can also be confronted with the false objections by which those who negate the divine attributes deny the divine essence itself. They must acknowledge the existence of the Lord, the Creator, which is known through the innate disposition with which people are created, necessary rational knowledge, conclusive rational proofs, the agreement of nations, and other evidence. They can then be challenged to establish an existence of the kind familiar to us, or an existence whose modality they know. They will inevitably have to resort to affirming something whose reality does not resemble other realities. Thus, what is said concerning all the other names and attributes by which He has described Himself follows the same principle as what is said concerning His very Self—glorified and exalted is He.

translated_text:
And the “crux of this discussion” is that most of those who deny some things indicated by the Quran and Sunnah while affirming others necessarily affirm something because there is a warrant for affirming it and no impediment, and deny something because an impediment exists or a warrant is absent. Or they suspend judgment when, in their view, there is neither a warrant nor an impediment. It should therefore be shown to such a person that a warrant exists for what he denies, just as it exists for what he affirms—either in every respect or in a respect that requires its affirmation. If the warrant is valid in the latter case, it is likewise valid in the former; otherwise, rejecting that warrant is no different from rejecting this one.

As for the impediment, it should be shown that the impediment he imagines in what he denies is of the same kind as the impediment he imagines in what he affirms. If that impediment—the alleged impossibility—is present on both suppositions, he does not escape the objection by affirming one and denying the other. If it is valid, it rules out both; if it is invalid, it rules out neither. He must therefore treat both alike in affirmation and denial. Since denial is untenable, affirmation is the only remaining course.

This is the crux of the argument that binds anyone who affirms anything. And everyone must either affirm something or be obliged to affirm it. This shows you, in general terms, that the consequences he claims require denial are unfounded imaginings, even without knowing in detail why they are unsound. As for the detailed argument, it establishes the invalidity of the impediment and the existence of the warrant, as has been explained on several occasions.

translated_text:
If someone who affirms those attributes which in us are accidents, such as life, knowledge, and power, but does not affirm those which in us are parts, such as the hand and foot, says, “These are components and parts that entail composition and corporeality,” he is told:

“Those, too, are accidents that entail corporeality and conceptual composition, just as, in your view, these entail composition perceptible to the senses.”

If he affirms those in a manner that does not make them accidents, or holds that calling them accidents does not preclude their affirmation, he is told:

“Then affirm these, too, in a manner that does not amount to composition and parts, or hold that calling them composition and parts does not preclude their affirmation.”

If it is said, “These can only be conceived of as components,” he is told, “Those can only be conceived of as accidents.”

If he says, “An accident is something that does not endure, whereas the Lord’s attributes endure,” the reply is:

“A part is something that can be separated from the whole, and that is impossible with respect to Allah. The separation of the eternal attributes from Allah Most High is absolutely impossible, whereas a created being’s accidents and parts may be separated from it.”

If he says, “That amounts to corporeality, and corporeality is ruled out,” the reply is: “This, too, amounts to corporeality, and corporeality is ruled out.”

translated_text:
If he says, “I can conceive of an attribute that is not an accident, subsisting in an entity that does not occupy space, even though it has no counterpart in the observable world,” he is told:

“Then conceive of an attribute which, in us, is a part, subsisting in an entity that does not occupy space, even though it has no counterpart in the observable world. For denying that this is conceivable amounts to denying that the other is conceivable. Even if there is a certain difference between them, it has no bearing on the point at issue.”

This is why the Jahmiyyah, who negate the divine attributes, deny them all. Yet that, too, entails denying the divine Essence. Those among their counterparts who affirm these attributes known through revelation explicitly describe them as attributes subsisting in Him, like knowledge and power. This, too, is neither the intelligible meaning of the revealed text nor what reason indicates. It is only necessity that has driven them into these straits.

The root of this is that they introduced expressions found neither in the Book nor in the Sunnah—broad, undifferentiated expressions such as “occupying space,” “bounded,” “body,” “composite,” and the like. They denied what these expressions signify and made that denial a premise accepted among themselves, regarding it as established by a certain form of reasoning. They were led into that reasoning by an approach they adopted to establish the temporal origination of the world through the temporal origination of accidents, or to establish the contingency of a body through its composition from parts. They were therefore compelled to extend the argument for temporal origination and contingency to everything falling within its scope, since a conclusive proof cannot be set aside in favour of a stronger opposing argument.

They then found that this created difficulties for them, both in relation to the revealed texts and, from another angle, in relation to reason. Thus they split into factions. Some give precedence to the first argument and reject whatever opposes it: these are the Muʿtazilah. Others give precedence to the second argument and reject the first

translated_text:
as did Hishām ibn al-Hakam, the Rāfidī. For it has been said that discussion of whether to deny or affirm that Allah is a body first arose in the time of Hishām ibn al-Hakam and Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf. Abū al-Hudhayl and other early Muʿtazilah denied that He is a body because of the reasoning they followed, whereas Hishām opposed them and affirmed that He is a body on the basis of the reasoning they had adopted. The former considered its affirmation impossible, while he considered its denial impossible. At other times, they reconcile the revealed texts with their reasoning in a manner whose impossibility and contradiction are apparent.

I know of no champion of speculative theology or philosophy who departs from the Book and the Sunnah without inevitably contradicting himself: he declares impossible the like of what he has deemed necessary, and deems necessary the like of what he has declared impossible. This is because their discourse comes from other than Allah. Allah Most High has said:

“Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would have found in it much inconsistency.”

The correct position is that of the imams of guidance: to describe Allah as He has described Himself, or as His Messenger has described Him, without going beyond the Quran and hadith, and to follow in this the path of the righteous predecessors, the people of knowledge and faith. The meanings understood from the Book and the Sunnah must not be rejected on the strength of specious objections, for that would amount to distorting words from their proper places. Nor should one turn away from those meanings and thus become like those who, when reminded of their Lord’s signs, respond to them with deafness and blindness. Nor should one abandon reflection upon the Quran and thus become like those who know nothing of the Scripture except wishful notions.

This, then, is the first of the two arguments: denying that these passages belong to those whose meaning is ambiguous.

The second argument:

If it is said that these passages are ambiguous, or that some of them are—as it is reported that some of the imams described certain passages cited by the Jahmiyyah as ambiguous—the response is this: the Quran’s statement that none but Allah knows its interpretation refers either to the ambiguous passages or to the entire Book, as explained earlier. Denying knowledge of its interpretation does not mean denying knowledge of its meaning, as we have already explained concerning the Resurrection and its events.

This argument is strong if Ibn Ishāq’s report concerning the delegation of Najrān is authentic: that they argued against the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, by citing the expressions “Indeed, We,” “We,” and the like. It is also supported by the established fact that the Quran contains ambiguous passages—that is, passages admitting two meanings. Some matters concerning the divine attributes fall into this category, just as matters concerning the Resurrection do—and all the more so. For the dissimilarity between Allah and His creation is far greater than that between what is promised in Paradise and what exists in this world.

The essential point of the answer, however, is what we stated at the outset: denying knowledge of the interpretation does not mean denying knowledge of the meaning. We further substantiate this by noting that Allah, glorified is He, says:

“We have certainly presented people with every kind of example in this Quran, so that they may take heed—an Arabic Quran, free from any crookedness, so that they may be mindful of Allah.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Alif Lām Rā. These are the verses of the clear Book. Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Quran so that you may understand.”

Thus, He states that He sent it down for them to understand, and that He sought for them to take heed.

He also says:

“These examples We present to people so that they may reflect.”

 وَأَيْضًا فَالسَّلَفُ مِنْ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالتَّابِعِينَ وَسَائِرِ الْأُمَّةِ قَدْ تَكَلَّمُوا فِي جَمِيعِ نُصُوصِ الْقُرْآنِ آيَاتِ الصِّفَاتِ وَغَيْرِهَا وَفَسَّرُوهَا بِمَا يُوَافِقُ دَلَالَتَهَا وَبَيَانَهَا وَرَوَوْا عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَحَادِيثَ كَثِيرَةً تُوَافِقُ الْقُرْآنَ وَأَئِمَّةُ الصَّحَابَةِ فِي هَذَا أَعْظَمُ مِنْ غَيْرِهِمْ مِثْلُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ مَسْعُودٍ الَّذِي كَانَ يَقُولُ:
 لَوْ أَعْلَمُ أَعْلَمَ بِكِتَابِ اللَّهِ مِنِّي تَبْلُغُهُ آبَاطُ الْإِبِلِ لَأَتَيْته. وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ عَبَّاسٍ الَّذِي دَعَا لَهُ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ
translated_text:
Thus He urged them to ponder it, comprehend it, understand it, take heed through it, and reflect upon it, without excluding any part of it. Indeed, several passages explicitly establish that this applies to the whole Quran, such as His words:

“Do they not ponder the Quran, or are there locks upon their hearts?”

And His words:

“Do they not ponder the Quran? Had it been from anyone other than Allah, they would surely have found many contradictions in it.”

Clearly, ruling out contradictions within it requires pondering it in its entirety. Pondering only part of it does not warrant concluding that the unexamined portions contain nothing that contradicts what one has examined.

When ‘Alī, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked, “Did the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, leave anything with you?” he replied:

“No, by Him who split the seed and created the soul, except an understanding of His Book that Allah grants a servant, and what is in this document.”

He thus indicated that understanding of the Quran varies within the Muslim community. Understanding is more specific than knowledge and judgment. Allah Most High says:

“We gave Solomon understanding of the matter, and to each We gave judgment and knowledge.”

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Many a transmitter understands better than a hearer.”

He also said:

“Convey from me, even if only a single verse.”

Furthermore, the early generations—the Companions, the Successors, and the rest of the Muslim community—discussed all the passages of the Quran, including the verses concerning the divine attributes and others. They explained them in accordance with what they signify and make clear, and narrated many hadiths from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that accord with the Quran. The leading Companions were foremost in this regard, such as ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, who used to say:

“If I knew of anyone more knowledgeable about Allah’s Book than myself whom I could reach by camel, I would go to him.”

And ‘Abd Allāh ibn ‘Abbās, for whom the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed

translated_text:
and who was the great scholar of the Muslim community and the interpreter of the Quran—these two, together with their students, were among the Companions and Successors who most firmly affirmed the divine attributes and most extensively transmitted reports concerning them from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Anyone acquainted with hadith and Quranic commentary knows this. Among the Successors, none were more distinguished than the students of these two eminent men. Indeed, the third alongside them, with regard to the foremost Successors, is of their kind or close to them. Comparable to their stature is that of the students of Zayd ibn Thābit. Yet, despite their distinction, his students did not study exclusively under him; they also learned from others, such as ‘Umar, Ibn ‘Umar, and Ibn ‘Abbās.

If the meanings of these verses were to be denied or left unspoken, the godly scholars among the Companions, those versed in the Book and the Sunnah, would not have been the ones who spoke most extensively about them. Moreover, the Companions reported that they learned the explanation of the Quran from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, along with its recitation. Not one of them ever reported that he declined to explain any verse.

Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said:

“Those who taught us the Quran—‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, and others—told us that whenever they learned ten verses from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, they would not proceed beyond them until they had learned the knowledge and practice they contained. They said, ‘Thus we learned the Quran, knowledge, and practice together.’”

Likewise, when the leading scholars were asked about any of these matters, they did not deny its meaning. Rather, they affirmed the meaning while disclaiming knowledge of how, as in the statement of Mālik ibn Anas when he was asked about His words,

" الِاسْتِوَاءُ مَعْلُومٌ "

 هَذَا ضَعِيفٌ؛ فَإِنَّ هَذَا مِنْ بَابِ تَحْصِيلِ الْحَاصِلِ فَإِنَّ السَّائِلَ قَدْ عَلِمَ أَنَّ هَذَا مَوْجُودٌ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَقَدْ تَلَا الْآيَةَ.

 ذِكْرُ الِاسْتِوَاءِ فِي الْقُرْآنِ وَلَا إخْبَارُ اللَّهِ بِالِاسْتِوَاءِ؛
 وَإِنَّمَا قَالَ:
translated_text:
exalted is He:

“The Most Merciful rose over the Throne.”

“How did He rise over it?” He replied: “Rising over is known; how is unknown. Believing in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation.” Rabī‘ah had said the same before him. People have accepted this statement, and no one among Ahl al-Sunnah rejects it. He made clear that rising over is known, just as everything else Allah has told us is known. Its manner, however, is unknown, and it is not permissible to ask about it: one must not ask, “How did He rise over it?” Mālik did not say that there is no manner; rather, he said that the manner is unknown.

There is disagreement about this among our associates and other scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah. Most of them, however, say: “His manner of being cannot be conceived by the mind, nor can His essential nature be expressed in words.” Some say: “He has neither a manner of being nor an essential nature.”

If it is said that his statement, “Rising over is known,” means that the occurrence of this wording in the Quran is known—as some of our associates have maintained, regarding knowledge of these meanings as part of the interpretation whose knowledge Allah has reserved to Himself—the reply is:

This is a weak explanation, for it merely states what is already known. The questioner already knew that this occurs in the Quran and had recited the verse.

Moreover, he did not say, “The mention of rising over in the Quran,” or, “Allah’s declaration that He rose over.” Rather, he said:

translated_text:
“Rising over is known.” He thus described the individual term as known, not the entire sentence.

Moreover, he said: “How is unknown.” Had he meant that, he would have said, “The meaning of rising over is unknown,” “The explanation of rising over is unknown,” or “What rising over signifies is not known.” He denied only knowledge of how He rose over, not knowledge of rising over itself.

The same applies to everything with which Allah has described Himself. If someone asked, concerning His words:

“Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing,”

“How does He hear, and how does He see?” we would reply: “Hearing and seeing are known; how is unknown.” If someone asked, “How did He speak directly to Moses?” we would reply: “Speaking is known; how is unknown.”

Furthermore, those among our associates and other scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah who have said this acknowledge that Allah is truly above the Throne, and that He Himself is above the Throne itself. They do not deny the meaning of rising over, nor do they consider it among the ambiguous passages whose meaning is entirely unknown. Moreover, the early generations agree on explaining it in accordance with the position of Ahl al-Sunnah.

Some of them said: “He rose above the Throne,” and “He was high above the Throne.” Others used different expressions. These explanations are reliably transmitted from the early generations; al-Bukhārī mentioned some of them in his Sahīh, towards the end of the Book of the Refutation of the Jahmiyyah. As for the interpretations that distort the meaning, such as “He took possession,” and the like, these are innovated interpretations introduced when the Jahmiyyah emerged.

Moreover, it is established that pursuing ambiguous passages is not confined to passages concerning the divine attributes. Indeed, Sahīh al-Bukhārī records that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Aisha:

“O Aisha, when you see those who pursue what is ambiguous in it, those are the ones Allah has named, so beware of them.”

This is general in scope. The account of Sabīgh ibn ‘Asal and Umar ibn al-Khattāb is among the best-known cases. News had reached Umar that Sabīgh was asking about the ambiguous passages of the Quran. When Umar eventually met him, Sabīgh asked him about:

“By the winds that scatter far and wide.”

Umar said, “What is your name?” He replied, “Allah’s servant, Sabīgh.” Umar said, “And I am Allah’s servant, Umar,” and beat him severely.

Whenever someone persistently questioned Ibn Abbas about a matter of this kind, he would say, “How much you need to be treated as Umar treated Sabīgh!” This was because they saw that the questioner’s purpose was to stir up discord, not to seek guidance and understanding. As the Prophet, blessings and peace be upon him, said:

“When you see those who pursue what is ambiguous in it.”

And as Allah Most High said:

“As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they pursue what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord.”

They therefore punished them for this corrupt intention, as in the case of someone who sets verses of the Quran against one another. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade this, saying:

“Do not set parts of Allah’s Book against one another.”

For that casts doubt into their hearts. Along with seeking discord, they sought its interpretation, which none but Allah knows. Their purpose was therefore blameworthy, and what they sought was unattainable—as with the trick questions that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbade.

translated_text:
Another illustration of the distinction between “meaning” and “interpretation” is that Sabīgh asked Umar about “those that scatter,” which is not a passage concerning the divine attributes. The Companions discussed its explanation. For example, when Ibn al-Kawwā’ asked Ali ibn Abī Tālib about it, Ali disliked his question because of the intention he perceived behind it. Ali’s subjects, however, were defiant toward him; he did not command the obedience Umar had enjoyed, which would have enabled him to discipline the questioner.

“Those that scatter,” “those that carry,” “those that glide,” and “those that apportion” contain ambiguity, because the wording could refer to winds, clouds, stars, angels, or other things: it does not name the things being described. The interpretation known only to Allah concerns the particular winds, their measure and characteristics, and when they blow; the particular clouds, the rain they carry, and when the rain falls. The same applies to “those that glide” and “those that apportion.” This is known only to Allah.

The same applies to His words “Indeed, We” and “We,” and similar designations of Allah that convey a plural sense—expressions such as the Christians pursued. Their referent is known: Allah, glorified is He. Yet a plural designation indicates a multiplicity of meanings, just as multiple names do, such as the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, the All-Hearing, and the All-Seeing. The One named is one, while the meanings of the names are multiple. The same is true of a designation expressed in the plural.

As for the interpretation whose knowledge Allah has reserved to Himself, it is the reality of His Essence and attributes, as Mālik said: “The manner is unknown.” Thus, if they ask, “What is the true nature of His knowledge, power, hearing, and sight?” the answer is: “This is the interpretation known only to Allah.”

translated_text:
How fitting it is to understand interpretation as referring to the Quran as a whole.

If it is objected, “But the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prayed for Ibn Abbās, ‘O Allah, grant him understanding of the religion and teach him interpretation,’” the answer is: He can know the interpretation of commands and prohibitions. The definite article here refers to the interpretation in question; the Prophet did not say, “the interpretation of the entire Quran.” The interpretation whose knowledge is denied to people concerns reports whose underlying reality is known only to Allah. The interpretation that can be known concerns matters whose interpretation people know. This is like His words:

“Do they await anything but its fulfillment? The Day its fulfillment comes…”

And His words:

“Rather, they have denied what they do not encompass in knowledge and whose fulfillment has not yet come to them.”

What is meant is the interpretation of reports concerning the future, for that is what is “awaited,” what “comes,” and what “has not yet come to them.” As for the interpretation of commands and prohibitions, that pertains to what is commanded. The interpretation of reports about Allah and those who lived in the past—if included under the term “interpretation”—is not something to be awaited.

Allah, glorified is He, knows best, and success comes through Him.

translated_text:
And the shaykh, imam, erudite scholar, exemplary guide, man of spiritual insight, jurist, hadith master, ascetic, worshipper, spiritual wayfarer, devout servant, mufti to the various groups, pillar of the Sharia, scholar of his age, peerless figure of his time, interpreter of the Quran, heir to the prophets, last of the jurists qualified for independent legal reasoning, Taqī al-Dīn Abū al-Abbās Ahmad ibn Abd al-Halīm ibn Abd al-Salām ibn Taymiyyah al-Harrānī—may Allah envelop him in His mercy—said:

Section: Oaths in the Quran

He, glorified is He, swears by certain things to affirm others. He swears only by His holy Self, characterized by His attributes, or by His signs, which necessarily point to His essence and attributes. His swearing by certain created things indicates that they are among His mighty signs.

the inviolable—and this too draws attention to a point. If He swears by it when it contains what is lawful, then it is all the more worthy of veneration when it contains what is inviolable. Likewise, if residence is intended, it is the negative sense, so the meaning is the same. [He has sworn by “the fig and the olive” and “this secure city.” The clause expressing what the oath affirms is stated in His saying, exalted is He:

“We have certainly created man in hardship.”

This means struggling with the affairs of this world and the Hereafter.] (*)

Such struggle entails strength on the part of the one engaged in it, together with much activity and resourcefulness. He therefore says, exalted is He:

“Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?”

“He says, ‘I have squandered vast wealth.’”

“Does he think that no one has seen him?”

This person is of the same kind as those nations, and of the same kind as the one who said:

“My wealth has availed me nothing. My authority has vanished from me.”

He possesses strength with which to contend with difficulties, yet He destroyed every one of them. Does he nevertheless think that no one will have power over him and requite him for his deeds? Does he think that no one has seen the wealth he squandered and thus knows what he has done?

Requital is accomplished through power and knowledge; indeed, everything is accomplished through them. His declaration, exalted is He, that He is powerful and knowing carries a warning and a threat. For if He has power, requital is possible; and if He has knowledge, requital is possible: He assesses what a person has done with justice. Anyone who lacks power and knowledge cannot requite, for someone who has no power over a person cannot

requite him. Someone who has power but does not see what the person has done would be unjust and transgressive if he requited him without knowledge. He must therefore know what that person has done. This is why a judge needs witnesses, and kings need administrative officials to inform them of the amounts of wealth and other matters, so that they may act with knowledge. . . . (1)

He states that He created man in hardship:

“Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?”

The particle lan negates a future occurrence. He is saying: Does he think that no one will have power over him in the future? This is why that man who feared his Lord and instructed his family to burn him and scatter his ashes knew that requital depended on power. He said:

“If Allah has power over me, He will surely punish me as He has punished no one in all the worlds.”

He, glorified is He, warns by mentioning His power because what He has power to do is connected with that power, just as He warns by mentioning His knowledge because requital takes place in conjunction with it. This occurs in His saying, exalted is He:

“Say, ‘He has power to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet.’”

When this was revealed, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “I seek refuge in Your Face; I seek refuge in Your Face.”

“Or to divide you into factions and make you taste one another’s violence.”

He said: “These two are less severe.”

This is because He mentioned His power and the kind of thing He has power to do, just as someone might say: “Where can you flee from me? I have the power to seize you.”

The same applies to knowledge through seeing, as in His saying here:

“Does he think that no one has seen him?”

translated_text:
and His saying, exalted is He, concerning the one who forbids a servant when he prays:

“Does he not know that Allah sees?”

And His saying, exalted is He:

“Say, ‘Work, for Allah will see your deeds, as will His Messenger and the believers.’”

And His saying:

“Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and private conversations? Indeed We do, and Our messengers are with them, recording.”

And His saying, exalted is He:

“Everything they have done is in the records.”

“And everything small and great is written down.”

There are other similar passages.

Mentioning that He sees deeds, knows them and keeps account of them entails a warning of requital for them. It is like someone saying, “I know what you have done, and reports of everything you have done have reached me,” and similar expressions. The purpose is not to speak merely of power or knowledge in isolation, but of power and knowledge associated with requital. Once knowledge and power are present, requital is possible and depends only on the will of the one who requites; nothing else is then needed. One must therefore seek salvation by asking His forgiveness, repenting to Him and doing good deeds that erase bad deeds.

Section

When He, glorified and exalted is He, swore by “those ranged in ranks,” “those that scatter” and “those sent forth,” He stated what the oath affirmed. He said, exalted is He:

“Indeed, your God is One.”

And He said, exalted is He:

“Indeed, what you are promised is true.”

“And Judgment will surely come to pass.”

And He said, exalted is He:

“Indeed, what you are promised will surely come to pass.”

He did not state what the oath affirmed in al-Nāzi'āt; for those ranged in ranks are the angels, and He did not swear to establish their existence, just as He did not swear to establish His own existence;

since the nations acknowledged those ranged in ranks, and knowledge of Him was manifest among them, requiring no oath. His oneness, however, was otherwise, for, as He, exalted is He, said:

“Most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him.”

Likewise, the nations generally acknowledge the angels. Allah mentioned that the people of Noah, ‘Ād, Thamūd and Pharaoh knew of the angels despite their associating partners with Him and rejecting the messengers.

The people of Noah said:

“This is only a man like yourselves who wishes to assert his superiority over you. Had Allah willed, He would have sent down angels.”

He, exalted is He, said:

“I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt that struck ‘Ād and Thamūd.”

“When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying, ‘Worship none but Allah,’ they said, ‘Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels.’”

Pharaoh said:

“Or am I not better than this one who is insignificant and can hardly express himself?”

“Then why have bracelets of gold not been bestowed upon him, or angels come with him in attendance?”

The same applies to the Arab polytheists. He, exalted is He, said:

“They say, ‘Why has an angel not been sent down to him?’ Had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided, and they would then have been granted no respite.”

He, exalted is He, said:

“They say, ‘What sort of messenger is this who eats food and walks in the markets? Why has an angel not been sent down to him to be a warner alongside him?’”

He, exalted is He, said of the nations in general:

“Nothing prevented people from believing when guidance came to them except that they said, ‘Has Allah sent a human being as a messenger?’”

“Say, ‘Had there been angels on earth, walking about at ease, We would have sent down to them from heaven an angel as a messenger.’”

Thus, these nations, which rejected the messengers and associated partners with their Lord, acknowledged Allah and His angels. How much more, then, would others do so? It is therefore clear that acknowledgment of the Lord and His angels is widespread among the nations. For this reason, He did not swear an oath to affirm it; rather, He swore to affirm His oneness, because most of them associate partners with Him.

Likewise, “those that scatter,” “those that bear,” and “those that sail” are things people witness, while “those who apportion affairs” are the angels. Thus, what He swore by did not itself include what He was affirming by the oath, so He stated what the oath affirmed. He, exalted is He, said:

“What you are promised is surely true, and judgment will surely come to pass.”

As for “those sent forth”—whether they are the angels descending with revelation, with the oath affirming recompense in the Hereafter, or the winds, or both—they too are known. As for “those who wrench out forcefully,” they are the angels who take souls. This entails recompense, which is among the greatest matters affirmed by these oaths.

He, exalted is He, said:

“Say, ‘The Angel of Death, who has been entrusted with you, will take your souls; then to your Lord you will be returned.’”

And He, exalted is He, said:

“Our messengers take his soul, and they never neglect their duty.”

“Then they are returned to Allah, their true Master.”

and this is certainty concerning what has been decreed but has not yet occurred, for seeking help and placing one’s trust in Allah concern only the future. As for what has already occurred, the response is patience, submission, and contentment, as in the hadith narrated by ‘Ammār ibn Yāsir, may Allah be pleased with him, and traced back to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“I ask You for contentment after Your decree has come to pass.”

Saying, “There is no might nor power except through Allah,” brings His help. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, prescribed it in response to the call to prayer. When the caller says, “Come to prayer,” the respondent says, “There is no might nor power except through Allah.” When he says, “Come to success,” the respondent says, “There is no might nor power except through Allah.”

The believer said to his companion:

“Why did you not say, when you entered your garden, ‘What Allah wills comes to pass; there is no power except through Allah’?”

For this reason, whoever fears the evil eye affecting something is instructed to say this. The expression “What Allah wills” means “What Allah wills comes to pass.” Thus, one does not consider oneself secure, but rather believes in divine decree and says, “There is no power except through Allah.”

In the hadith narrated by Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī, may Allah be pleased with him, and recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“It is a treasure from among the treasures of Paradise.”

A “treasure” is wealth already amassed that needs no gathering. This is because these words express reliance upon Allah Most High and utter need of Him. It is well known that nothing occurs except by Allah’s will and power, and that nothing comes from created beings except what Allah brings about in them. Thus, when the heart ceases seeking

help from them and seeks it from Allah, it has sought it from the Creator of that help, who alone can provide it.

Allah Most High says:

“Whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold; and whatever He withholds, none can release thereafter.”

And He says:

“If Allah touches you with harm, none can remove it except Him; and if He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty.”

And He says:

“If He touches you with good, He has power over all things.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? If Allah intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?’”

The man mentioned in Surah Yā-Sīn said:

“Shall I take gods besides Him? If the Most Merciful intends harm for me, their intercession will avail me nothing, nor can they save me. I would then be in manifest error.”

For this reason, Allah commands people in numerous passages to place their trust in Him alone. A report states:

“Whoever wishes to be the strongest of people, let him place his trust in Allah; and whoever wishes to be the richest of people, let him have greater confidence in what is in Allah’s hand than in what is in his own.”

Allah Most High says:

“Place your trust in the Ever-Living, who does not die, and glorify Him with praise. Sufficient is He as One fully aware of His servants’ sins.”

Allah Most High has commanded that He be worshipped and trusted. He says:

“So worship Him and place your trust in Him.”

And He says:

“Say, ‘He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.’”

Moses said:

“O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then place your trust in Him, if you are Muslims.”

And Shuayb said:

“My success is only through Allah. In Him I have placed my trust, and to Him I turn in repentance.”

The believers said:

“Our Lord, in You we have placed our trust, to You we turn in repentance, and to You is the final return.”

Allah Most High says:

“Remember the name of your Lord and devote yourself wholeheartedly to Him. He is the Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but Him, so take Him as your Trustee.”

And He says:

“Whoever fears Allah, He will make a way out for him and provide for him from where he does not expect. Whoever places his trust in Allah, He is sufficient for him. Allah will surely accomplish His purpose. Allah has set a measure for everything.”

In this regard, people fall into four groups:

One group neither worships Him nor places its trust in Him. These are the worst of creation.

Another group seeks to worship Him by doing what He has commanded and refraining from what He has forbidden, but they have not fully realized trust in Him and dependence on His help. They are therefore unable to accomplish much of what they seek and lose heart in many afflictions.

Among these are those who deny divine decree and regard themselves as the originators of their own actions. In reality, they neither seek His help nor ask Him to reform their hearts, set them straight, or guide them. These people are forsaken, just as the Muslim community regards them.

Others affirm divine decree in both word and belief, yet this belief has not taken hold of their hearts in knowledge and practice as has their intention to perform purification and prayer. These too are weak and helpless.

One of these people may therefore be granted powers of influence, whether to subdue his enemy or support his ally, just as kings are granted such powers. He may also be granted some disclosure of hidden matters, either through information conveyed to him by some jinn—whether or not he knows that they are jinn—or by other means.

One of these people may say, “I receive from Allah, while others receive from Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.” His own state in this regard and what sets him apart lead him to see that the powers of influence and disclosures granted to him come through a path other than that of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. In this he speaks the truth. Yet these things are, in reality, a source of ruin for him.

For if someone acts without the command of the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and takes what the Messenger has not permitted him; appoints and dismisses, gives and withholds without the Messenger’s command; kills and strikes without his command; honours and humiliates without his command; and receives an inward address containing commands and prohibitions, believing that Allah has commanded and forbidden him without the Messenger’s mediation—then this entire state of his comes from Satan. It is Satan who commands and forbids him: Satan commands him, and he acts, imagining that he is acting by Allah’s command.

By my life, he does act by Allah’s command governing creation and destiny, through the intermediary of Satan’s command, as Allah Most High says concerning sorcerers:

“They cannot harm anyone through it except by Allah’s permission.”

Likewise, the believer acts by Allah’s command governing creation and destiny, but through the intermediary of the command of the Messenger, who conveys it to him from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

translated_text:
Thus, for him, what is lawful is what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful; what is forbidden is what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden; and religion is what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed. The other person, by contrast, does not look to the Messenger for the commands and prohibitions he receives inwardly, or for what he does and commands others to do.

This type is common among shaykhs concerned with the heart and spiritual states whose knowledge of the Quran and Sunnah and adherence to the Messenger are weak. They are dominated by what they find in their hearts and the commands they receive inwardly, whether these agree with the Messenger or contradict him.

They vary in this according to their closeness to the Messenger or their distance from him. Many have strayed so far from him that they see fit to help the unbelievers fight the Muslims, believing that Allah, glorified be He, has commanded them to do so. They also believe that Ahl al-Suffa (the People of the Portico) did this. Some hold that the Messenger was not sent to them and their like, but only to ordinary people. Others believe that the Messenger was subordinate to Ahl al-Suffa, while they had no need of him. There are other such types, who have become numerous in these times.

translated_text:
All these people claim knowledge of spiritual reality, saying: “Spiritual reality is one thing, and the revealed Law is another.” They share two characteristics: they possess powers and spiritual unveilings beyond those of ordinary people, and they refuse to weigh these against the Quran and Sunnah or submit them to the Messenger’s judgment.

They are like kings who govern their kingdoms without following the commands of Allah and His Messenger. Yet none of these kings says, “Allah commanded me to do this,” or “I am an ally of Allah,” or “I receive spiritual support from Allah independently of the Messenger,” or “The messengers were not sent to people like me.” Kings merely pursue their own ends without making them a religion. These people, however, turn their own ends—which involve some of the gravest injustice and corruption, indeed even unbelief—into a religion practised by those whom they regard as Allah’s allies.

This is because these things come to them through a kind of asceticism and worship. Yet it is not the asceticism and worship with which Allah sent His Messenger. Rather, it resembles the condition of the People of the Book and the polytheists, such as the devotees of India, the Christians, and others like them. Thus their resemblance to the devotees among the polytheists and the People of the Book becomes apparent. Indeed, someone who had seen the devotees of India and then saw the ecstatic devotees of the house of al-Rifā'ī found their presence in Muslim lands objectionable. He said: “These are exactly like the pagan devotees of India.”

translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām said:

In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

My Lord, make this easy and help me by Your mercy.

All praise is due to Allah. We seek His help and forgiveness, and we seek refuge in Allah from the evil within ourselves and from our evil deeds. Whoever Allah guides, none can lead astray, and whoever He leads astray, none can guide. I bear witness that none has the right to be worshipped except Allah alone, without partner, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger. May Allah bless him and grant him peace.

To proceed: One of the brothers asked me to write him an introduction setting out general principles that would help him understand the Quran, its interpretation and its meanings; distinguish truth from the various kinds of falsehood in both transmitted reports and reasoned explanations concerning it; and identify the decisive evidence by which to judge between differing views. For books of Quranic commentary are filled with both the worthless and the valuable, blatant falsehood and manifest truth. Knowledge consists either of an authenticated report from one protected from error or of a statement supported by established evidence,

and anything beyond these is either spurious and rejected or left undecided, its soundness or falsity unknown.

The Muslim community urgently needs to understand the Quran, which is Allah’s firm rope, the wise reminder, and the straight path. Through it, desires do not lead astray and tongues do not become confused. It never wears out through repeated recitation, its wonders never cease, and scholars never have their fill of it. Whoever speaks according to it speaks the truth; whoever acts upon it is rewarded; whoever judges by it judges justly; and whoever calls to it is guided to a straight path. Any tyrant who abandons it, Allah will crush; and whoever seeks guidance elsewhere, Allah will lead astray.

Allah Most High says:

“Then if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor fall into misery. But whoever turns away from My remembrance will have a life of hardship, and We will raise him blind on the Day of Resurrection. He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’ He will say, ‘Just as Our signs came to you and you forgot them, so today you will be forgotten.’”

Allah Most High also says:

“There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book, through which Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace, brings them out of darkness into light by His permission, and guides them to a straight path.”

Allah Most High also says:

“Alif Lām Rā. This is a Book We have sent down to you so that you may bring people out of darkness into light, by their Lord’s permission, to the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy—Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth.”

Allah Most High also says:

“And thus We have revealed to you an inspiration by Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor faith, but We have made it a light by which We guide whomever We will among

Our servants. And indeed, you guide to a straight path—the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on earth. Truly, all matters return to Allah.”

I have written this brief introduction as Allah Most High has enabled me, setting down what my heart dictated. Allah is the Guide to the path of right guidance.

Section

It must be understood that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, explained the meanings of the Quran to his Companions just as he taught them its wording. Allah Most High’s words,

“So that you may explain to people what has been sent down to them,”

embrace both.

Abū ‘Abd al-Rahmān al-Sulamī said: “Those who taught us the Quran, such as ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Mas‘ūd, and others, told us that when they learned ten verses from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, they would not go beyond them until they had learned the knowledge and practice they contained. They said, ‘Thus we learned the Quran, knowledge, and practice together.’”

For this reason, they would spend a considerable time memorizing a surah. Anas said: “When a man had read al-Baqarah and Āl ‘Imrān, he rose in our esteem.” Ibn ‘Umar spent several years memorizing al-Baqarah—eight years, it is said—as Mālik related.

This was because Allah Most High said:

“This is a blessed Book which We have sent down to you so that they may reflect upon

its verses.”

He also said:

“Then do they not reflect upon the Quran?”

And He said:

“Then have they not reflected upon the Word?”

Reflecting upon speech is impossible without understanding its meanings. Likewise, Allah Most High said:

“Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Quran so that you may understand.”

Grasping speech necessarily entails understanding it. It is well known that the purpose of all speech is to understand its meanings, not merely its wording; this applies all the more to the Quran. Moreover, ordinary practice makes it inconceivable that people would read a book in a field of knowledge, such as medicine or arithmetic, without seeking an explanation of it. How much more so with the speech of Allah, which safeguards them and upon which their salvation, happiness, and well-being in both their religious and worldly affairs depend?

For this reason, disagreement among the Companions over the interpretation of the Quran was very rare. Although it was more common among the Successors than among the Companions, it was still slight compared with that of later generations. The more virtuous the age, the greater its unity, harmony, knowledge, and clarity of explanation.

Some of the Successors received the entire explanation of the Quran from the Companions. As Mujāhid said: “I went through the Quran with Ibn ‘Abbās, stopping him at each verse and asking him about it.” For this reason, al-Thawrī said: “If an interpretation comes to you from Mujāhid, that is sufficient for you.” Thus al-Shāfi‘ī, al-Bukhārī, and other scholars rely on his interpretation. Likewise, Imam Ahmad and others who compiled works of Quranic interpretation cite chains of transmission from Mujāhid more frequently than from anyone else.

Section

Disagreement among the early generations over Quranic interpretation was slight, and their disagreements over legal rulings were more numerous than their disagreements over interpretation. Most disagreements authentically reported from them involve variation rather than contradiction. This is of two kinds:

The first is when each expresses the intended meaning in different words, indicating a different aspect of the same referent. This resembles co-referential names, which fall between synonyms and terms with distinct referents—as with the names given to a sword: “the keen blade” and “the Indian blade.” Such are the Most Beautiful Names of Allah, the names of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the names of the Quran. All of Allah’s names refer to the same One, so invoking Him by one of His Most Beautiful Names does not contradict invoking Him by another. Rather, it is as the Most High says:

“Say, ‘Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever name you call Him by, His are the Most Beautiful Names.’”

Thus, the All-Knowing denotes the Essence and knowledge; the All-Powerful denotes the Essence and power; and the Most Merciful denotes the Essence and mercy. Whoever denies that His names signify His attributes, while claiming to uphold the apparent meaning, speaks in a manner akin to the extremist Qarmatian esotericists, who say: “One must say neither that He is living nor that He is not living.” Rather, they deny both contradictory alternatives concerning Him. These Qarmatian esotericists do not reject a name that merely identifies, as pronouns do; they reject the positive attributes contained in His Most Beautiful Names. Whoever agrees with their objective thus agrees with the extremist esotericists in this respect, despite claiming strict adherence to the apparent meaning. This is not the place to elaborate on that. The point is simply that each of His names denotes His Essence and the attributes it contains.

It also denotes, by necessary implication, the attribute contained in another name. The same applies to the names of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, such as Muhammad, Ahmad, al-Māhī, al-Hāshir, and al-ʿĀqib; and likewise to the names of the Quran, such as the Quran, the Criterion, the Guidance, the Healing, the Clear Exposition, the Book, and others of this kind.

If the questioner’s purpose is to identify what is named, we may refer to it by any name, provided that the referent of that name is known. The name may be a proper name or a description. For example, someone might ask about His words:

“And whoever turns away from My remembrance”

“What is meant by His remembrance?” He may be told, for example: “It is the Quran,” or: “It is the Books He has revealed.” For “remembrance” is a verbal noun, and a verbal noun is sometimes grammatically linked to the one performing the action and sometimes to its object.

Thus, when “remembrance of Allah” is used in the second sense, it means the words by which He is remembered, such as a servant’s saying: “Glory be to Allah; praise be to Allah; there is no god but Allah; Allah is the Greatest.” When used in the first sense, it means what He Himself mentions—that is, His speech. This is what is meant in His words:

“And whoever turns away from My remembrance”

For He says before this:

“Then if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer.”

His guidance is the remembrance He has revealed. After this, He says:

“He will say, ‘My Lord, why have You raised me blind when I used to see?’”

“He will say, ‘Thus did Our signs come to you, but you forgot them.’”

The point is to determine whether “remembrance” means His revealed speech or the servant’s remembrance of Him. Whether “My remembrance” is explained as “My Book,” “My speech,” “My guidance,” or something similar, the referent is the same.

If, however, the questioner wishes to know the particular attribute conveyed by a name, something more is needed than merely identifying its referent. Someone might, for example, ask about al-Quddūs, al-Salām, and al-Mu’min while already knowing that these names refer to Allah. What he wishes to understand, however, is what it means for Him to be Quddūs, Salām, Mu’min, and so forth.

Once this is understood, the early generations often referred to the same entity using an expression that identifies it, even though that expression conveys an attribute not conveyed by another name. This is like someone saying that Ahmad is al-Hāshir, al-Māhī, and al-‘Āqib, and that al-Quddūs is the All-Forgiving

to one and the same thing, but each described it by one of its attributes.

The Second Category

Each interpreter mentions some of the kinds encompassed by a general term, by way of illustration and to draw the listener’s attention to that kind—not as a definition exactly coextensive with what is being defined. This is like a non-Arabic speaker asking what the word “bread” denotes, then being shown a loaf and told, “This.” The indication is to this kind of thing, not to that particular loaf alone.

An example is what has been transmitted concerning His words:

“Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants. Among them are those who wrong themselves, those who take a middle course, and those who are foremost in good deeds.”

It is well known that “those who wrong themselves” includes those who neglect obligatory duties and commit forbidden acts. “Those who take a middle course” includes those who fulfil obligatory duties and refrain from forbidden acts. “Those who are foremost” includes those who advance ahead, drawing near to Allah through good deeds in addition to obligatory duties. Those who take a middle course are the people of the right:

“And the foremost will be the foremost.”

“Those are the ones brought near.”

Each interpreter then applies this to a particular kind of obedience. For example, one says that the foremost is someone who prays at the beginning of the prescribed time; the one who takes a middle course prays within that time; and the one who wrongs himself delays the afternoon prayer until the sun turns yellow.

Another says that Allah mentioned the foremost, the one who takes a middle course, and the wrongdoer at the end of Sūrat al-Baqarah. He mentioned the benevolent person who gives charity, the wrongdoer who consumes usury, and the just person who engages in trade. In matters of wealth, people are either benevolent, just, or unjust. Thus, the foremost is the benevolent person who performs

recommended deeds as well as obligatory ones; the wrongdoer is someone who consumes usury or withholds zakat; and the one who takes a middle course pays the obligatory zakat and does not consume usury. There are other statements of this kind. Each statement mentions a particular kind encompassed by the verse, to show the listener that the verse includes it and, through it, draw attention to similar cases. Explaining by example can be easier than giving an abstract definition.

A sound mind recognizes the general kind, just as it does when someone points to a loaf and says, “This is bread.” Their statement, “This verse was revealed concerning such-and-such,” often belongs to this category, especially when a particular person is mentioned. Examples include the occasions of revelation mentioned in Quranic commentary: their statements that the verse concerning zihār was revealed concerning the wife of Aws ibn al-Sāmit; that the verse concerning mutual imprecation was revealed concerning ‘Uwaymir al-‘Ajlānī or Hilāl ibn Umayyah; and that the verse concerning kalālah was revealed concerning Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh.

They also say that His words:

“And judge between them by what Allah has revealed”

were revealed concerning Banū Qurayzah and Banū al-Nadīr; that His words:

“Whoever turns his back to them on that day”

were revealed concerning the Battle of Badr; and that His words:

“When death approaches any of you, let there be witnesses among you”

were revealed concerning the case of Tamīm al-Dārī and ‘Adī ibn Badā’. There is also Abū Ayyūb’s statement that His words:

“Do not cast yourselves into destruction with your own hands”

“were revealed concerning us, the Ansār”—and the rest of the hadith. There are many similar examples in which they mention that a passage was revealed concerning a group of polytheists in Mecca, a group from the People of the Book—Jews or Christians—or a group of believers.

translated_text:
Those who said this did not mean that the verse’s ruling applied exclusively to those particular individuals and no one else, for no Muslim or rational person would say such a thing. Although scholars have disputed whether general wording revealed on a particular occasion is restricted to that occasion, no Muslim scholar has held that the general statements of the Quran and Sunnah apply exclusively to the particular individual concerned. The most that is argued is that they are restricted to the category to which that individual belongs, thus encompassing others like him, rather than having the full general scope of their wording.

If a verse revealed on a particular occasion contains a command or prohibition, it applies both to that individual and to others in the same position. Likewise, if it contains a statement of praise or blame, it encompasses both that individual and others in the same position.

Knowing the “occasion of revelation” helps one understand the verse, for knowledge of the cause leads to knowledge of its effect. Hence, the sounder of the two juristic opinions is that, when an oath-taker’s intention is unknown, one refers to the reason for his oath and what prompted and provoked it. Their statement, “This verse was revealed concerning such-and-such,” sometimes means that this was the occasion of its revelation, and sometimes means that it falls within the verse’s scope, even if it was not the occasion of revelation—just as one might say, “This verse refers to such-and-such.”
